articles.title: 'Water is our red line': Shehbaz Sharif threatens India with 'direct response' over Indus Treaty
articles.summary: Pakistan News: Pakistan has yet again raked up India’s suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), with its Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif threatening a “direct resp.
articles.body: Pakistan has yet again raked up India’s suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), with its Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif threatening a “direct response” to New Delhi’s move, which came days after the Pahalgam terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir in April last year."The Prime Minister said that India has proven itself an enemy of peace by unilaterally and illegally suspending the Indus Waters Treaty. He announced that every drop of Pakistan's water is our red line. There will be no compromise on the water issue. If India does not come to the right path, we will give it a direct response," the Pakistan Prime Minister's Office said in a statement on X.Sharif, speaking at an event on the eve of Pakistan’s Independence Day (August 14), sought to portray India as an “enemy of peace” over New Delhi’s decision to keep the IWT in abeyance following the April 22 Pahalgam terror attack, in which 26 civilians were killed.He said New Delhi had proved itself an “enemy” of peace by putting the treaty in abeyance."India proved itself an enemy of peace by unilaterally and illegally suspending the Indus Waters Treaty. I declare in clear terms that every single drop of Pakistan's water is our red line. If India does not come to its senses, it will be responded to directly," the Pakistani premier added.The military hostilities ended on May 10 after Islamabad sought a ceasefire following India’s air strikes on multiple Pakistani air bases. The conflict erupted after India's Operation Sindoor in retaliation for the Pahalgam attack.New Delhi kept the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance after a Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) meeting on April 23, 2025, and asserted that the conditions under which the treaty was negotiated have "fundamentally changed."India has asserted the treaty can no longer function in its present form and will remain in abeyance until Pakistan “credibly and irrevocably” ends its support for cross-border terrorism.The Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) was signed in September 1960.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Belgian student in construction job uncovers €9m gold treasure while digging sewer trench
articles.summary: Europe News: An ordinary summer job turned into a real life treasure hunt for an 18-year-old Belgian student, Kobe, after he stumbled upon a hidden hoard of gold w.
articles.body: An ordinary summer job turned into a real life treasure hunt for an 18-year-old Belgian student, Kobe, after he stumbled upon a hidden hoard of gold worth an estimated €9 million while digging trenches for a new sewage system.According to The Guardian, Kobe was working with colleagues at the construction site when they spotted the objects while laying drainage pipes, initially unaware that they had stumbled upon a fortune.First appeared to be a handful of €1 coins soon turned out to be gold coins, nuggets and numbered bullion bars concealed inside a bricked in cellar wall beneath a grand villa. The extraordinary discovery was made at the site of a former brewery on Van Langenhovestraat in Sint-Gillis-Dendermonde, around 30km north-west of Brussels.The treasure was deliberately concealed inside a bag placed within a bricked-in cellar wall beneath a grand villa. The hidden hoard included gold coins, nuggets and numbered bullion bars, with its total value estimated at around €9 million.Kobe and his colleagues immediately alerted the police after stumbling upon the gold hoard. CAW Oost-Vlaanderen, the social welfare organisation carrying out the renovation of the property, was informed about the discovery. The entire treasure has since been moved to a secure facility in Brussels, where authorities are conducting a detailed investigation to determine its legal ownership.The discovery has now opened a complex legal question over who can claim the fortune. Hanne Ollevier of the East Flanders public prosecutor’s office said authorities must first establish that the bullion was not stolen property or the proceeds of criminal activity. The investigation will also have to determine whether the building contractors, CAW Oost-Vlaanderen or descendants of the Van Assche family could have a claim to the treasure.A possible clue to the treasure’s origins has emerged from the history of the Van Assche family. Piet Buyse, a former mayor of Dendermonde, said the family’s fortune had “certainly stayed in the family” and suggested it would not be surprising if they had converted at least some of their wealth into gold and hidden it in a safe place.For Kobe and his colleagues, the sheer scale of the discovery made it clear that the treasure had to be handed over to the authorities. Kobe said they understood immediately that a find of this magnitude could not simply be kept. “If it had been a few coins, maybe not,” he said, adding that they may eventually receive some kind of finder’s reward.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Meet Ni Jingchen: The 12-year-old Beijing student who posted a strange fossil online and helped reveal Asia’s first Jurassic amphibian footprint
articles.summary: China News: In early 2025, 12-year-old Ni Jingchen was out exploring with his parents in Beijing's Mentougou district when he noticed two tiny marks on a slab of .
articles.body: In early 2025, 12-year-old Ni Jingchen was out exploring with his parents in Beijing's Mentougou district when he noticed two tiny marks on a slab of exposed rock. Ni already loved fossils and knew enough to realise that the strange impressions were worth a closer look, so he photographed them and shared the find online. He had no idea that his casual discovery would eventually bring professional palaeontologists to the site and reveal something scientists had never documented in Asia before. Associate professor Xing Lida of the China University of Geosciences in Beijing saw the photographs and organised a team to investigate. Their analysis showed that the slab preserved a forefoot and hind-foot track made by a small amphibian roughly 160 million years ago, during the Middle Jurassic. The animal most likely belonged to Salamandroidea, the group that includes modern salamanders, making Ni's find the first scientifically described Jurassic amphibian track record from China and Asia. This remarkable find highlights how youthful curiosity and careful observation can meaningfully advance scientific understanding, proving that groundbreaking discoveries sometimes begin with everyday exploration.Why the tiny tracks had never been recorded anywhere in Asia beforeBefore this discovery, Jurassic vertebrate track records from the Beijing region were dominated by dinosaurs and turtles, with no amphibian tracks reported. The new fossil consists of two impressions preserved on a single slab near Jiulong Road in Longquan town, Mentougou district. Researchers interpreted them as a connected forefoot-hind-foot pair, probably produced by the same animal as it moved across the sediment. The better-preserved forefoot measures about 1.5 centimetres long and 1.3 centimetres wide and shows four slender, pointed digits arranged in a fan-like pattern. The hind-foot impression is less clearly preserved and contains five indistinct digit traces. Their relative size, spacing and orientation support the interpretation that the two impressions were produced by the same animal.How researchers identified the tracks as belonging to a salamander-like amphibianTo extract as much detail as possible from marks barely larger than a fingernail, the research team used photogrammetric three-dimensional modelling to build high-resolution digital reconstructions of the tracks, allowing them to examine subtle surface features. The findings were formally published in the paper Possible caudata tracks from the Middle Jurassic Yaopo Formation in Beijing, China in the peer-reviewed journal Ichnos. After comparing the morphology of the impressions with known amphibian tracks, the researchers concluded that the trackmaker most likely belonged to Salamandroidea, a group that includes modern salamanders and related tailed amphibians. The tracks come from the Middle Jurassic Yaopo Formation, a coal-bearing geological unit in the Mentougou area that has also yielded plant fossils including ferns, ginkgoes and cycads. Taken together, the evidence indicates that small, land-adapted amphibians lived in what researchers interpret as a lake-swamp environment in the region roughly 160 million years ago.Why Ni's discovery shows how amateur fossil hunters can contribute to scienceThe discovery began not with a professional fossil survey but with a schoolboy who noticed something unusual in an exposed rock surface. After Ni shared photographs of the specimen online, Xing Lida became aware of the find and led the subsequent investigation. Xing has described the discovery as an example of public participation in paleontological research, particularly highlighting how young fossil enthusiasts can contribute to science when they pay close attention to geological exposures.For scientists, the significance extends beyond the novelty of finding two tiny tracks. The fossil provides direct evidence that amphibians occupied Middle Jurassic landscapes in northern China and adds a previously missing component to the region's vertebrate track record. The authors say further discoveries from the Yaopo Formation could help researchers reconstruct the area's ancient environment in greater detail, including the diversity of animals that inhabited the plant-rich lake and swamp ecosystems that existed around 160 million years ago.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Dhaka terms UN’s report on al-Qaida presence in B’desh ‘assumption-driven’
articles.summary: Dhaka, Bangladesh on Monday termed a recent UN Security Council report on Al-Qaeda's attempt to establish cells in the country as \"assumption-driven\",
articles.body: Dhaka, Bangladesh on Monday termed a recent UN Security Council report on Al-Qaeda's attempt to establish cells in the country as "assumption-driven", saying the government is not taking any action based on the report.The 38th report of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team submitted to the Security Council 1267 Sanctions Committee concerning ISIL and Al-Qaeda said that there was some concern about Al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent (AQIS) "trying to exploit Bangladesh to establish cells there.""We are not taking this (report) into consideration. I have not read the report yet. Besides, as far as I have heard, it says they have assumed that such a thing could happen. So, we are not taking any action based on an assumption-driven report," Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed told reporters while replying to questions.The report, which was issued and circulated among member states last week, said that "AQIS continued to evolve from a fragmented group into a regional terrorist entity."AQIS established logistics and financial networks, working in decentralised small, scattered cells instead of large units. The attack in November 2025 on the Red Fort in Delhi was officially attributed to AQIS," it said.Bangladesh police have said they had no specific info on AQIS cell risk.But a senior Counter Terrorism and Transnational Crime (CTTC) unit officer of police, speaking on condition of anonymity, told the Daily Star that Bangladesh's counter-terrorism capacity suffered over the last two years, when an interim regime largely ran the country.The Muhammad Yunus-led interim administration assumed power after a violent street protest toppled then-prime minister Sheikh Hasina's government on August 5, 2024. The interim regime continued until the elections on February 12, which installed Tarique Rahman's government.According to the paper, the CTTC official said that "experienced teams were weakened and surveillance on terrorism suspects released on bail was curtailed" during the past two years.Bangladesh last month ordered a nationwide security alert, particularly asking police to take care of their own personnel and vehicles, while a separate order was issued to heighten security at airports.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Women were excluded from Liechtenstein’s throne for more than 400 years; a new royal rule now gives the firstborn child, regardless of gender, the right to inherit, and know who'll now own the throne
articles.summary: Europe News: Several European nations have female leaders next in line for the throne, but one of them has recently initiated the norm. Liechtenstein has become th.
articles.body: Several European nations have female leaders next in line for the throne, but one of them has recently initiated the norm. Liechtenstein has become the latest country to amend its royal rules and allow women to take the throne. During its national day celebrations on Saturday, August 15, the country announced the change.“The order of succession is being changed from male primogeniture to absolute primogeniture,” the House of Liechtenstein said in a statement. “This means that in future the first-born child, regardless of sex, will become heir to the throne and later princess or prince of Liechtenstein.”The decision will not affect the current leadership of the nation of just 44,00 people. Liechtenstein is a tiny, doubly landlocked country tucked away between Switzerland and Austria, whose ruler enjoys sweeping political powers, unlike many of his counterparts in Europe. The current ruler is Prince Hans-Adam II, 81, who has been the head of the royal family since 1989. On Liechtenstein's national day 22 years ago, August 15, 2004, Prince Hans-Adam named his eldest child, Hereditary Prince Alois, as his regent. This means that, for the past two decades, Prince Alois, 58, has overseen most official royal duties while Prince Hans-Adam remains the official monarch and head of state. (Prince Hans-Adam’s father, the late Prince Franz Joseph II, did the same for him in 1984, five years before his death.)The rule change does not apply to the current members of the royal family. It will go into effect for the future descendants of Prince Alois and his wife, Princess Sophie. The couple shares Prince Joseph Wenzel, 31, Princess Marie Caroline, 29, Prince Georg Antonius, 27, and Prince Nikolaus Sebastian, 25. As of now, Prince Joseph is in the line of succession after his father.“With this change in the law, we want to ensure that both the Principality of Liechtenstein and the Princely House are led by the person who has been best prepared for this responsibility,” said Prince Alois in a statement as per a report by PEOPLE.Rule changes allowing for female monarchs are becoming more common around the world. Several European nations currently have a female next in line to the throne, including Sweden’s Crown Princess Victoria, Belgium’s Princess Elisabeth, Spain’s Princess Leonor and the Netherlands’ Princess Catharina-Amalia. In 2011, Great Britain and the rest of the Commonwealth made the Perth Agreement, which replaced male-preference primogeniture with absolute primogeniture, which does not take sex into account in the line of succession. This meant that when Prince Louis was born in April 2018, Princess Charlotte did not move below him, making her the first British princess in history to rank above her brother.However, hesitation to change the rules has led to looming questions about succession in other countries like Japan. In July, the Japanese parliament passed a bill allowing distant male relatives over 15 to be adopted into the imperial line of succession. The rule change , the first amendment to the main text of the Imperial House Law since 1949, comes amid concern about dwindling male heirs.However, no changes have been made to the law that prevents women from inheriting the throne, meaning that Emperor Naruhito’s only child, Princess Aiko, is still ineligible to succeed her father on the throne. Currently, the emperor’s 60-year-old brother, Fumihito, also known as Crown Prince Ashikino, is in line to inherit, followed by his 19-year-old son, Prince Hisahito. Interestingly, per the BBC, recent polls indicate that a majority of Japanese citizens would be in favour of a female empress.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Move Imran Khan to hospital': Pakistan Supreme Court directs govt amid ex-PM's health concerns
articles.summary: Pakistan’s Supreme Court on Tuesday directed the government to move imprisoned former prime minister Imran Khan to a hospital, meeting a longstanding
articles.body: Pakistan’s Supreme Court on Tuesday directed the government to move imprisoned former prime minister Imran Khan to a hospital, meeting a longstanding demand from his party and family amid growing concerns over his health.Khan, 73, has been in jail since August 2023 after being convicted in several cases that he and his supporters have described as politically motivated. His Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party welcomed the court order, saying it should have come earlier.“It’s a very welcome order and we wish it had happened sooner so his eye and general health would not have deteriorated this much,” PTI spokesperson Zulfikar Bukhari told Reuters.“He should remain in hospital until all doctors are satisfied,” Bukhari added.According to Khan’s spokesperson Naeem Haider Panjutha, the court directed that he be moved to Shifa International Hospital within 48 hours and remain there until September 16.Also Read: 'Needs to be moved to hospital now': Imran Khan's health in jail deterioratesThe order came amid renewed concerns over Khan’s physical and mental health. His sons, Sulaiman Khan and Kasim Khan, have repeatedly raised concerns about his access to family, lawyers and doctors.“We have no updates because his family, doctors and lawyers haven’t been allowed to see him for seven months,” they told CNN earlier this month.The development came after former Pakistani president Arif Alvi also said on Tuesday that Khan’s medical reports were “alarming”, citing concerns over anxiety, palpitations and high blood pressure.In a post on X, Alvi said, “Imran Khan’s medical reports are alarming. I have gone through them with several specialists, and I am writing this in plain language so every Pakistani can understand exactly what is happening.”Alvi said the issues that concerned him most were Khan’s “anxiety and stress levels”, “palpitations,” and “high blood pressure”.Alvi also raised concerns over Khan’s heart rate and called for further medical monitoring, including a 24-hour Holter monitor.“I am deeply worried. Isolation is taking a physical toll on his body. If this is not addressed immediately, the damage may become irreversible with more complications to follow,” Alvi said.Calling for Khan to be hospitalised, the former president said: “@ImranKhanPTI definitely needs to be moved to a hospital environment now, under an independent panel of doctors.”Khan’s legal troubles intensified after his ouster as prime minister in a no-confidence vote in 2022. He has faced multiple cases, including those involving state gifts and an unlawful marriage, with some convictions suspended or overturned and appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing.The PTI, which came to power in 2018 and retains a significant support base, was stripped of its election symbol before the 2024 general election, forcing its candidates to contest as independents.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Blast near Kabul school injures around 50 children; UN condemns 'heinous' act
articles.summary: South Asia News: A hand grenade explosion near a school in Kabul’s predominantly Hazara neighbourhood of Dasht-e-Barchi injured several children on Monday afternoon, a.
articles.body: A hand grenade explosion near a school in Kabul’s predominantly Hazara neighbourhood of Dasht-e-Barchi injured several children on Monday afternoon, according to Afghan authorities and local media reports.Kabul police spokesman Khalid Zadran confirmed that “a number of children” were wounded and said an investigation was underway, without giving further details.Local media reports put the number of injured at around 50 children, though the figure has not been independently verified.Reports said the blast occurred around 4.30pm local time near the Shama-e Hidayat school, with several injured students taken to a nearby hospital.The cause of the explosion was reported as a hand grenade by Kabul Now and TOLOnews, but authorities have not publicly provided further details on who was behind the attack.The blast took place in Dasht-e-Barchi, a western Kabul district largely populated by members of Afghanistan’s Hazara minority, who have faced repeated attacks and discrimination.The Islamic State’s Khorasan branch (ISIS-K) has previously targeted Hazaras, including in attacks on schools, mosques and other civilian sites.UN special rapporteur on Afghanistan Richard Bennett condemned the attack, calling it “heinous” and saying an independent investigation was needed to hold those responsible to account. “Once again this mainly Hazara part of Kabul has been targeted. Deplorable!” he wrote.In May 2021, three bombings outside a school in Dasht-e-Barchi killed dozens of people, most of them young girls from the Hazara community. No group has been identified as responsible for Monday’s blast in the reports provided.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ‘All trade, commercial exchanges halted’: How UAE responded to Iran’s latest ballistic missile attack
articles.summary: The United Arab Emirates has suspended all trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran after accusing Tehran of launching two
articles.body: The United Arab Emirates has suspended all trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran after accusing Tehran of launching two ballistic missiles towards the Gulf state, dealing a fresh blow to efforts to ease tensions between the two countries.The UAE defence ministry said its air-defence systems detected two ballistic missiles launched from Iran towards its territory on Tuesday. The incident triggered an emergency alert on residents' phones and was described as the first direct Iranian attack on the UAE since May.The ministry later said its assessment indicated that the missiles had been targeting maritime traffic. One missile fell into the sea outside the UAE's territorial waters, while the other fell within them. No damage or injuries were reported.UAE freezes economic ties with TehranFollowing the missile incident, the UAE foreign affairs ministry announced that it was halting economic engagement with Iran until further notice.The ministry said that “in light of regional escalations that undermine regional and international peace and security, all trade, commercial exchanges, and financial transactions with Iran have been halted until further notice”.The decision threatens to reverse a gradual restoration of economic and diplomatic links between Abu Dhabi and Tehran. Trade between the UAE and Iranian ports had resumed in some areas, while certain Iranian flights to the UAE had also quietly returned.The emergency alert issued on Tuesday was the first such warning in several months, apart from a false alert in June. Dubai's financial district had also begun filling up with bankers, while Emirati authorities had started allowing some 20,000 Iranian residents who were outside the country when the war began to return to the UAE.Iran denies launching missilesIran has denied the UAE's accusation, with Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei rejecting the claim and warning that such allegations could undermine regional efforts to rebuild trust.Baghaei “completely rejected” the UAE's claim and expressed regret over the accusations against Iran, according to a statement issued by the Iranian Foreign Ministry.“This behaviour is contrary to the principle of good neighbourliness and disrupts ongoing efforts to strengthen trust between regional countries and prevent the escalation of insecurity in the region,” Baghaei said.The Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson also called on regional countries to refrain from making “baseless accusations” against Tehran.“The Foreign Ministry spokesman called on all regional parties to refrain from making baseless accusations against the Islamic Republic of Iran, considering the existing complexities due to the ongoing evils of the US and the Zionist regime against regional peace and security, especially the history of numerous false flag operations,” he said.The UAE defence ministry, meanwhile, maintained that its air-defence systems had detected the missiles.“The first fell outside the country's territorial waters, while the second fell within its territorial waters,” the UAE Ministry of Defence said in a post on X.The UAE military said its forces remained on high alert and were prepared to respond to threats against the country's security and sovereignty.Missile attack threatens fragile UAE-Iran thawThe latest confrontation comes after more than two months of efforts by Abu Dhabi and Tehran to reduce tensions that had escalated following the US and Israeli war against Iran that began on February 28.During the conflict, Iran launched repeated missile and drone attacks against neighbouring Gulf states, including the UAE, accusing them of enabling US and Israeli military operations.The UAE was among the Gulf states most heavily targeted, sustaining almost 3,000 missile and drone attacks. Abu Dhabi also carried out scores of strikes against Iran, taking a more hawkish position towards Tehran than several of its Gulf neighbours.Tensions later eased after Washington and Tehran reached a memorandum of understanding in June. However, the agreement began to unravel in early July, after which Iran shifted much of its military focus towards Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan.In recent months, the UAE had sought to rebuild diplomatic and economic channels with Iran while maintaining close military ties with Israel and the United States. Emirati officials have repeatedly said they want to avoid being drawn further into a wider regional conflict.That balancing act is now under growing pressure following the latest missile incident.Strait of Hormuz tensions add to pressureThe confrontation also comes amid escalating tensions around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial route for global oil and natural gas shipments.The UAE accused Iran earlier this month of attacking ships operated by Abu Dhabi National Oil Company in the strategic waterway. Tehran has also maintained restrictions on traffic through the strait while issuing increasingly aggressive military rhetoric.A separate maritime incident was reported on Tuesday when an unidentified projectile struck a ship as it sailed out of the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Oman. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre said the strike damaged the vessel's engine room and caused a casualty, while the Omani Coast Guard assisted other crew members.Another cargo vessel was struck by multiple projectiles about 40 nautical miles, or 74 kilometres, southeast of Mokha in Yemen and was declared a “constructive total loss”, according to the British maritime monitoring agency. The agency did not identify the projectiles or those responsible.The incidents have added to concerns over the safety of commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Red Sea region, both vital routes for global trade.Trump tensions with Oman over Iran dealThe maritime crisis has also drawn Oman into a dispute between Washington and Tehran over arrangements for shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.US President Donald Trump threatened Oman after becoming dissatisfied with an emerging agreement between Muscat and Tehran aimed at managing ship traffic through the strategic waterway, according to two regional officials cited by The Associated Press.The officials said the Trump administration objected to parts of the proposed agreement, including joint Iranian and Omani management of the exit route from the strait and voluntary fees on vessels linked to security and maritime environmental protection.Trump on Monday threatened to bomb Oman as it worked with Iran on an agreement intended to reopen the strait and potentially allow Washington and Tehran to resume negotiations aimed at ending the conflict.He later posted a map on social media depicting the Strait of Hormuz as US territory. Trump had previously floated the idea during an Oval Office exchange, saying, “I like the idea of declaring it a territory,” without providing further details.The White House referred to Trump's earlier Oval Office remarks when asked about the latest comments and declined to provide additional details.Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi responded to Trump's remarks on social media.“Just as Trump correctly wrote the name of the eternal Persian Gulf, his delusion regarding the Strait of Hormuz will soon either be corrected, or we will correct this deluded man’s delusions for him,” Gharibabadi wrote on X.Trump has previously threatened Oman over its dealings with Iran. In May, he told reporters during a Cabinet meeting that Oman “will behave just like everybody else, or we will have to blow them up.”Iran says Strait will not reopen yetIran has maintained that the Strait of Hormuz will not fully reopen until Washington meets its conditions, including commitments related to sanctions, frozen assets and military operations.“Until the United States fulfills its commitments under the agreement, including lifting the blockade, releasing frozen assets, lifting oil sanctions, ending threats and military operations on all fronts, and implementing the other conditions to which it committed, the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen,” Iranian parliamentary speaker and former US-Iran negotiator Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf said.Trump, however, said on Tuesday that the United States had no planned talks with Iran and insisted that the strait was “open and operating”, despite limited maritime traffic and reports of fresh attacks.He also said the US blockade of the waterway remained “in full force and effect” and claimed that all water mines had been removed.Egypt has backed the Iranian-Omani negotiations, saying an agreement could help create conditions for Washington and Tehran to return to talks.The Egyptian foreign ministry said the agreement could pave the way for a “comprehensive and permanent deal that addresses all concerns and enhances regional security and stability."The latest developments leave the UAE facing renewed security pressure as its decision to suspend economic ties with Iran threatens to derail a fragile diplomatic thaw, while tensions around the Strait of Hormuz and wider regional military activity continue to intensify.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Don't let them win': Netanyahu's party puts Zohran Mamdani alongside Iran, Hezbollah leaders on billboard
articles.summary: Middle East News: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party has stepped up its attack on New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, placing his image alongside I.
articles.body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party has stepped up its attack on New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, placing his image alongside Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on a campaign billboard in Tel Aviv.The billboard, displayed in central Tel Aviv, carries the message, “They want Netanyahu to lose … Don’t let them win.”The poster features the logo of Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party, according to The Guardian and the New York Post.Netanyahu shared an image of the billboard on his social media accounts on Sunday, along with a video highlighting Mamdani’s criticism of the Israeli prime minister.Why Netanyahu is targeting MamdaniThe billboard is the latest escalation in an increasingly bitter public feud between Netanyahu and Mamdani, who has been a vocal critic of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza.Mamdani last month called Netanyahu a “war criminal” who “belonged in The Hague” and urged US authorities to enforce the International Criminal Court's arrest warrant against the Israeli leader if he travels to New York for the UN General Assembly in September.Netanyahu responded by accusing Mamdani of “fomenting hate” and turning different religious groups against each other in New York.The Israeli prime minister has also argued that progressive Democrats associated with Mamdani are putting at risk what he described as traditionally bipartisan US political support for Israel.However, recent polling cited by The Guardian has indicated that Mamdani is more popular among American Jews than Netanyahu.Billboard comes as Netanyahu enters election campaignThe attack comes as Netanyahu seeks another term amid a politically challenging environment in Israel.Israel's parliament, the Knesset, was dissolved in July, paving the way for elections in October — the first national election since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023.Netanyahu's right-wing coalition is trailing in some opinion polls, according to The Guardian.The prime minister has increasingly invoked Mamdani's criticism of him as part of his campaign messaging. The billboard is not the first Likud campaign material to use the New York mayor's comments against Netanyahu.Mamdani has not publicly responded to the latest billboard.Feud comes amid tensions over Gaza ceasefireThe exchange comes as US-Israeli efforts to advance a Gaza ceasefire deal remain stalled.US President Donald Trump's son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner held a three-hour meeting with Netanyahu on Monday, but the talks produced no breakthrough.Israel has continued to insist that its forces will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas agrees to disarm, according to The Guardian.Netanyahu's latest attack on Mamdani also follows his controversial description of Britain as “the Islamic republic of Britain” in an interview with Israel's army radio. He also called the UK the “first Islamic republic to get a nuclear weapon”, remarks that drew criticism for echoing a far-right trope about Britain's Muslim population.For Netanyahu, the Mamdani billboard therefore serves two purposes: attacking one of his most prominent US critics while portraying the New York mayor as part of a broader political camp he says is hostile to Israel.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A 2,500-year-old sacred well in Italy hid bronze offerings and two human skeletons from an ancient Etruscan ritual
articles.summary: Europe News: Archaeologists have uncovered an unusual ritual well at Kainua, an ancient Etruscan city near Marzabotto in northern Italy, offering new insights into.
articles.body: Archaeologists have uncovered an unusual ritual well at Kainua, an ancient Etruscan city near Marzabotto in northern Italy, offering new insights into the rituals surrounding its foundation. The remarkable discovery was first made during the University of Bologna’s 39th excavation campaign in the city’s sacred urban area, dedicated to the goddess Uni. At the bottom of the well, researchers found two bronze female statuettes and a rare bronze plate, all remarkably well preserved. According to Alma Mater Studiorum, Università di Bologna (University of Bologna, Italy), these objects are interpreted as votive offerings placed during a foundation ritual between the end of the 6th and the first decades of the 5th century BC. Two adult human skeletons were also discovered and are associated with the ritual closing of the structure. The findings suggest that the well was far more than a simple source of water for the community. Instead, it formed part of a complex religious practice connected with water, sacred urban space and the foundation of the Etruscan city.Bronze offerings found in a sacred well reveal Kainua’s earliest religious traditionsThe newly discovered well was found in the sacred urban area of Kainua, where archaeologists have identified monumental temples associated with major Etruscan deities. The University of Bologna excavation, directed by Elisabetta Govi, uncovered the structure during its 39th campaign at the site. The well contained three objects, including two female bronze statuettes and a rare bronze plate.Their remarkable preservation has allowed researchers to see the metal's original shiny appearance. The excavation team says the objects were not ordinary items left behind. They were votive offerings placed during a solemn foundation ceremony. The ritual dates to between the late 6th century and the early decades of the 5th century BC, around the time when Kainua was founded.What the ritual well reveals about water and Etruscan religionThe location of the well helps explain why archaeologists believe it may have held religious significance. Kainua’s sacred urban area was home to two imposing temples associated with Tinia and Uni, the supreme divine couple. Tinia corresponds broadly to Zeus or Jupiter, while Uni is associated with Hera or Juno. The area dedicated to Uni also provides evidence for the cult of Vei, linked with agricultural and human fertility. Within this landscape, water appears to have held more than a practical role.Two human skeletons mark the ritual closing of the wellThe human remains are among the most striking aspects of the discovery. The excavation announcement describes two adult human skeletons associated with the ritual closure of the well. Current evidence does not conclusively show that these individuals were victims of human sacrifice. Instead, the archaeologists interpret their presence as part of an act that marked the end of the structure’s ritual use.The sequence is particularly significant as votive objects were placed at the bottom when the well was founded, and human remains were associated with its closing. Together, the findings indicate a defined ceremonial life. They also provide new evidence of how Etruscan communities connected construction, water and religious practices with the foundation of an urban settlement.What the discovery reveals about Etruscan city foundationsThe discovery offers further insight into how Etruscan cities were founded and how religious practices shaped their early development. Kainua has been excavated by the University of Bologna since 1988, and the latest campaign was supported by a €140,000 grant from the Directorate General of Museums of Italy’s Ministry of Culture.The additional funding allowed researchers to extend the 2026 excavation by two weeks, allowing researchers to investigate the area further. The newly found objects are expected to be added to the National Etruscan Museum of Marzabotto, known as MNEMA. For archaeologists, the well is valuable because its intact artefacts and their positions preserve evidence of a ritual sequence.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Sheikh Hasina says she will return to Bangladesh in December. What awaits her back home
articles.summary: South Asia News: For the first time since fleeing Bangladesh two years ago, Sheikh Hasina has put a specific month on her planned return: December.In July, nearly a mo.
articles.body: For the first time since fleeing Bangladesh two years ago, Sheikh Hasina has put a specific month on her planned return: December.In July, nearly a month before the second anniversary of the fall of her government, the 78-year-old former prime minister said she intended to return to Bangladesh in December along with senior Awami League leaders and surrender to the courts.On August 5, the second anniversary of the collapse of her government, Hasina repeated that pledge despite the enormous legal and political risks involved.She has already been sentenced to death in absentia over crimes against humanity linked to her administration’s crackdown on the July 2024 uprising, in which up to 1,400 people were killed, according to UN estimates. Hasina has rejected the charges and has described the proceedings against her as "politically motivated."The question now is not simply whether she will follow through on her return plan. It is what she hopes to achieve by announcing it and what awaits her if she goes back.A return plan and a high-stakes gambleHasina’s announcement is striking because the risks of returning are unusually high.She herself has acknowledged that she could be arrested or even killed.“They (Bangladesh government) may arrest me on my return, they may even kill me. Still, I have to go. If death comes, I want it to come on my own soil, where my parents are buried and where their blood was shed,” the former prime minister said on August 5, referring to the 1975 assassination of her parents and three of her four siblings by a group of army officers.Her December plan therefore leaves her facing difficult choices.If she returns, she could be taken into custody almost immediately and remain out of active politics for an extended period. If she stays in India, meanwhile, she remains vulnerable to accusations from opponents that she is unwilling to face the legal process at home.By naming December, however, Hasina has also put a clear timeline on her own political future and brought the question of her return back into Bangladesh’s political debate.Whether or not she ultimately follows through, the announcement keeps attention on both her and the Awami League at a time when the party has little room to operate politically.The Awami League’s activities were first banned under the Muhammad Yunus-led interim administration in 2025, and the restrictions were subsequently given legal backing by parliament in 2026.Politics behind Sheikh Hasina’s Bangladesh return planThrough her remarks from India, Hasina has continued to present herself both as a prime minister whose government was toppled and as a victim of what she describes as a foreign-backed conspiracy.Her August 5 address, at a virtual press conference in New Delhi, followed a similar pattern. She criticised Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s government and called for the ban on the Awami League to be lifted.Her proposed return also has obvious implications for the party.It gives Awami League supporters a rallying point and keeps Hasina at the centre of discussions about the party’s future, despite the legal risks she faces if she goes back.A political leader can remain influential even without holding office, particularly when supporters continue to identify strongly with that leader and believe the political system has treated the party unfairly.Hasina’s announcement, therefore, serves another purpose: it prevents her from disappearing from the political conversation while the Awami League remains barred from normal political activity.Sheikh Hasina return: What could unfold in BangladeshHasina has made a dramatic return from exile once before.In 1981, after nearly six years abroad following the assassination of most of her family, she returned to Bangladesh from India as the newly elected president of the Awami League.Then, large crowds gathered to welcome her.This time, the circumstances could hardly be more different.Anti-Hasina sentiment remains strong, even though her father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, occupies a central place in Bangladesh’s independence history.Hostility towards the Awami League has also extended beyond the former prime minister herself.For instance, the family home of Shakib Al Hasan, one of Bangladesh’s most celebrated cricketers and a former Awami League MP, was targeted with petrol bombs just hours after his virtual appearance in the August 5 media interaction.Awami League leaders themselves acknowledge the possibility of violence if senior figures, particularly Hasina, return.“We will have to face whatever happens... There will be a backlash because the extremists are highly weaponised. We are preparing for this,” senior party leader Mohibul Chowdhury said a day after Hasina announced her return plan.On its part, the incumbent government led by Tarique Rahman, son of Hasina’s longtime political rival Khaleda Zia, has little obvious political incentive to make her return easy.The Awami League government was removed after a mass uprising, and the political order that followed has been built partly around a rejection of Hasina’s rule.The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) government has already indicated that she would be arrested if she returns.Her arrival could therefore become an immediate test of how the government handles both the legal process against her and the political consequences that could follow.Banned and bruised: What happens to Awami LeagueAlthough Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was among the Awami League’s co-founders, the party gradually became synonymous with Sheikh Hasina, who has been its undisputed leader for more than four decades.Her political future is therefore tied to another question: can the party survive without her?The Awami League’s organisational strength was heavily dependent on Hasina’s leadership. Since her departure, with several senior leaders also in exile, underground or in custody, no obvious figure has emerged who appears capable of filling the political space she left behind.Her children do not offer an obvious alternative either.Her son, Sajeeb Wazed Joy, a dual US-Bangladeshi citizen, was previously involved with the Awami League and served as an adviser to his mother, but has not emerged as her political successor. Her daughter, Saima Wazed, meanwhile, has remained away from politics and is a senior World Health Organization official.That makes Hasina’s continued political activity important for the Awami League.Her return pledge gives supporters something to rally around at a time when the party remains politically marginalised.But it also creates a dilemma.A comeback centred entirely on Sheikh Hasina could keep the Awami League’s identity alive, but it could also make it harder for the party to develop new leadership and a new political message.The environment that sustained Hasina for years has changed sharply. Public resentment towards her remains strong, while the legal cases and allegations of abuses against her government have made any political comeback far more difficult.What lies ahead for Sheikh HasinaSince late 2024, Dhaka has been seeking Hasina’s extradition from India, while New Delhi has said the requests are being examined under established legal processes.Bangladesh has also linked progress on her extradition to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s proposed maiden official visit to India.A voluntary return by Hasina could remove one of the most contentious issues in India-Bangladesh relations, although it would not by itself resolve the wider strains between the two governments.Whether she actually follows through on her December pledge remains uncertain.If she does return, the immediate risks are clear: arrest, incarceration and possibly, the enforcement of a death sentence handed down in absentia.Her presence could also reignite political tensions in a deeply divided country.At the same time, returning would give Hasina something she currently lacks from exile — a chance to physically reconnect with supporters and place herself once again at the centre of Bangladesh’s political drama.December, therefore, could become a defining moment for Sheikh Hasina. It could mark the beginning of a comeback or the end of her career as an active political force.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1966, a 71-year-old woman donated nearly 100 acres of her Virginia farm and money for an amphitheatre; the land became America's only national park dedicated to the performing arts
articles.summary: US News: Before it became a stage beneath the stars, Wolf Trap was simply a Virginia farm. But in the 1960s, one woman had a very different dream for the land:.
articles.body: Before it became a stage beneath the stars, Wolf Trap was simply a Virginia farm. But in the 1960s, one woman had a very different dream for the land: a place where music, theater and the performing arts could be part of America’s national park system. Meet Catherine Filene Shouse, a prominent Washington arts advocate and a political insider. A generous gift of land and money helped her vision become a reality: Wolf Trap National Park for the Performing Arts in Fairfax County, Virginia, the only national park in the United States dedicated to the performing arts. Scroll down to read the details.A vision born of an arts renaissanceAccording to the Wolf Trap website, Shouse came up with the idea of a performing arts park in 1964, when excitement about culture was building in Washington, DC. The movement had been gathering momentum during the administration of President John F. Kennedy who championed the arts as an important aspect of American public life. One early harbinger of that change occurred at Kennedy’s 1961 inauguration, when the poet Robert Frost was asked to take part in the ceremony. Shouse was well-connected in Washington's political and cultural circles. Later, she sat on the original Board of Trustees of the Kennedy Center, which gave her the interest and contacts to take on an ambitious national arts project. According to experts, her proposal came at a time when public institutions were looking for ways to open up the arts to wider audiences.Secretary Udall’s Role in Support of the ArtsAnother major player in Washington’s cultural transformation was Secretary of the Interior Stewart L. Udall. Udall, who worked for both Kennedy and President Lyndon B. Johnson, advocated for more government funding for the arts and humanities. His work also included historic venues and major institutions of culture.One of Udall’s major projects was the reopening of Ford’s Theatre. The building had mainly served as a museum since President Abraham Lincoln was assassinated there in 1865, while its stage remained closed for more than a century. Working with Senator Milton R. Young, Udall helped secure funding for its rehabilitation. Ford’s Theatre finally reopened in 1968, 103 years after Lincoln’s assassination. Udall also played a role in the development of what would become the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.New stages were filling WashingtonShouse’s idea came during a broader expansion of performing arts venues across Washington. The Merriweather Post Pavilion in Columbia, Md., was built and opened in 1967. The outdoor space was associated with the National Symphony Orchestra, and had permanent seating and a large lawn. Washington already had major venues, such as Constitution Hall and the Carter Barron Amphitheater. Constitution Hall opened in 1929 and became an important concert hall. The Carter Barron Amphitheater opened in Rock Creek Park in 1950. In its heyday, the outdoor theater featured some major performers including Ella Fitzgerald, Louis Armstrong and Diana Ross and the Supremes among others. It is run by the National Park Service. But Shouse wanted something else: a permanent performing arts destination attached directly to the national park system.Virginia Farm to National ParkAccording to the website, before she approached the National Park Service, Shouse had offered Wolf Trap Farm to the National Symphony Orchestra as a performing arts park. The proposal was rejected partly due to concerns about the property's accessibility. Shouse didn’t give up. Eventually her plan gained support from Washington’s cultural and political establishment. On October 15, 1966, Congress approved legislation establishing Wolf Trap Farm Park in Fairfax County, Va.The legislation designated the site as a location for performing arts, educational programming and recreation. At the age of 71, she donated nearly 100 acres of her farm and contributed to building an amphitheater, turning private land into a public cultural center.A stage like no other national parkWolf Trap eventually became known for its outdoor performances and its unique relationship between nature and the arts. The park's most famous venue, the Filene Center, offers shows in an open-air setting where music and theater are enjoyed by audiences steeped in the landscape. It was a curious extension of the national park idea to create it. Wolf Trap showed that the arts themselves could be the main reason for a national park, not simply the preservation of historic sites, dramatic landscapes or natural wonders. Today, the Washington area has an immense variety of cultural venues ranging from historic theaters to concert halls, clubs and large entertainment arenas. These include the National Theatre, Howard Theatre, The Fillmore, 9:30 Club, Capital One Arena, and other major performance venues. Yet Wolf Trap remains the only national park in the United States dedicated to the performing arts, carrying forward the vision Shouse first championed more than six decades ago. What began as one woman’s dream for a Virginia farm has become a national treasure, giving audiences the rare opportunity to experience performances beneath the open sky.Images Courtesy: Wolf Trap Instagram and Dumbarton OaksCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Florida police officer arrested after using Flock surveillance cameras 717 times to track estranged wife
articles.summary: A Florida police officer has been arrested after allegedly using his department's Flock licence-plate surveillance system 717 times to track a vehicle
articles.body: A Florida police officer has been arrested after allegedly using his department's Flock licence-plate surveillance system 717 times to track a vehicle belonging to his estranged wife over nearly two years. Christopher Goodson, a 31-year-old officer with the Haines City Police Department, allegedly searched the vehicle's licence plate between September 1, 2024, and June 30, 2026, both while on and off duty, according to an arrest affidavit. Investigators said he used department-issued devices and entered various law-enforcement justifications for the searches, even though his estranged wife was not involved in a criminal investigation. Goodson was charged with official misconduct and an offence involving computer systems and was placed on paid administrative leave. He has also indicated that he plans to resign. The case has also drawn attention to the privacy risks posed by law-enforcement surveillance tools when access is used for personal purposes rather than legitimate investigations. This case underscores growing concerns about accountability and oversight mechanisms needed to prevent officers from exploiting powerful surveillance databases for personal, non-investigative purposes. The case highlights how powerful surveillance technology can become a serious privacy threat when safeguards and professional boundaries are ignored.Florida police officer allegedly tracked estranged wife 717 timesInvestigators reviewing Goodson's activity on the Flock system found 717 searches involving the licence plate associated with his estranged wife's vehicle between September 2024 and June 2026. The searches were reportedly carried out using his police credentials and department-issued devices. According to the arrest affidavit, Goodson accessed the system both while working and while off duty. Investigators found particularly high numbers of searches during several months in 2025, including 280 searches in September alone. The repeated searches became the focus of a criminal investigation into whether the officer had improperly used a law-enforcement database for personal purposes.The investigation began after Goodson told a supervisor that he had conducted searches involving his estranged wife's vehicle. According to the affidavit, his wife had told him that The Washington Post had contacted her about an investigation into the alleged tracking. Goodson then reportedly acknowledged that he had used the Flock system to determine the location of his children when they were with their mother. The department subsequently reviewed his Flock activity and found hundreds of searches connected to the vehicle.Investigators say he entered false reasonsAccording to the arrest affidavit, Goodson allegedly selected different law-enforcement justifications when conducting the searches. These included reasons related to wanted persons, drugs and narcotics, criminal motor vehicle offences, assault and battery, fleeing and eluding, traffic infractions, larceny and theft and felony investigations. Investigators reportedly found no evidence that his estranged wife was the subject of a legitimate criminal investigation during the period examined. Her vehicle was also not identified as being connected to a crime that would have justified the searches.The investigation found that Goodson allegedly used department-issued equipment and his employee credentials to access the Flock system. The searches were made both while he was on duty and during periods when he was off duty, according to investigators. This distinction became important because the system is intended to support legitimate police investigations rather than personal matters. The department has said officers are expected to use investigative databases only for authorised law-enforcement purposes.Goodson said he was trying to locate his childrenGoodson reportedly told his supervisor that he used the Flock system to keep track of his children when they were staying with their mother. His explanation is included in the investigative record, but authorities allege that the searches were not legitimate law-enforcement queries. The investigation instead focused on whether he had used his official access to obtain information about his estranged wife's vehicle for personal reasons.Florida officer faces two chargesGoodson was arrested on August 11, 2026, and charged with one count of official misconduct and one count involving unauthorised use of computer systems, networks and electronic devices. Local reports citing the arrest affidavit describe both charges as third-degree felonies. The allegations have not been proven in court, and Goodson is presumed innocent unless and until he is found guilty. Reports also said it was unclear whether he had entered a plea or retained an attorney to comment publicly on the allegations.Police officer placed on paid administrative leaveFollowing the investigation, the Haines City Police Department placed Goodson on paid administrative leave. He had joined the department in March 2022 and has indicated that he intends to resign. Police Chief Isaac Jackson described the incident as unfortunate and said the department does not tolerate the misuse or unauthorised use of investigative databases. The chief also stressed that police information systems are intended for legitimate official purposes and must be accessed according to department policies and applicable law.The Haines City Police Department has said it will introduce additional quarterly reviews of employees' access to investigative databases. The reviews are intended to identify searches that may not have a legitimate law-enforcement purpose and strengthen accountability around sensitive information. Despite the controversy, the department has indicated that it will continue using Flock technology because officials consider automated licence-plate readers a useful investigative tool when they are used properly.What are Flock surveillance cameras?Flock's system consists of automated licence-plate-reader cameras that photograph passing vehicles and use computer vision technology to identify licence plates and other vehicle characteristics. The resulting information can be stored in a searchable database that allows authorised law-enforcement users to look for previous sightings of a vehicle. Police departments can use the technology to investigate stolen vehicles, missing people and other cases. However, the ability to search historical vehicle sightings has also raised concerns about privacy and potential misuse.Goodson's arrest comes amid wider scrutiny of automated licence-plate-reader networks in the US. A Washington Post investigation published in August 2026 identified at least 50 law-enforcement officers who had been accused or charged with misusing licence-plate-reader systems, including cases involving alleged surveillance of romantic partners and former partners. The investigation highlighted concerns about how officers can access large databases containing information about where vehicles have been detected.Privacy concerns surrounding licence-plate readersThe controversy centres on the amount of information that automated licence-plate readers can make searchable. A single camera captures a vehicle at a particular location, but a large network can potentially create a detailed record of where that vehicle has been seen over time. Supporters argue that the technology can help police solve crimes more efficiently, while critics say strong safeguards are needed to prevent it from becoming a tool for monitoring people without a legitimate law-enforcement reason.Flock has faced calls to strengthen controls over how police officers use its systems. The Washington Post reported that the company introduced an audit-assistance feature designed to identify potentially suspicious activity, including repeated searches of the same vehicle and searches conducted outside an officer's normal working hours. Such tools are intended to help agencies identify unusual patterns and investigate potential misuse of the system.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Steve Jobs’ 8th-grade science project becomes an auction sensation as bids reached $8,475
articles.summary: Tech News News: Long before Steve Jobs helped build Apple into one of the world’s most influential technology companies, he was already experimenting with electronics.
articles.body: Long before Steve Jobs helped build Apple into one of the world’s most influential technology companies, he was already experimenting with electronics. A science project Jobs created while he was in eighth grade has now resurfaced decades later, offering collectors a rare glimpse into his early interest in technology. The project, titled “What is the Silicon-Controlled Rectifier?”, is part of an auction of Steve Jobs and Apple memorabilia marking Apple’s 50th anniversary. The collection includes vintage computers, signed documents, advertising material and other objects connected to Jobs and Apple’s early history. The school project reflects the hands-on curiosity that would later become a defining part of Jobs’ approach to technology and design.From Steve Jobs’ school science fair project to a sought-after piece of Apple historyThe project dates to February 29, 1968, when Jobs was an eighth-grade student. Rather than producing a conventional school display, he chose to explore the silicon-controlled rectifier, or SCR, a semiconductor device used to control electrical power. The surviving project consists of a large tri-fold display explaining the technology, along with demonstration circuits designed to show how the component worked. It also includes a written report and circuit diagrams created by Jobs. The project offers an unusually personal connection to Jobs because it predates the formation of Apple by several years. At the time, he was still a school student experimenting with electronics, long before he became associated with the development of personal computing. One small detail makes the project even more distinctive. Jobs left instructions for the science fair judges explaining how to use the circuits and reminding them to unplug the equipment afterwards. The warning suggests that the young Jobs was already paying close attention to how his technical work should be handled.The project stayed with the Jobs family for decadesUnlike many school projects that disappear after a science fair ends, this one remained within Jobs’ family for decades. According to a report by AppleInsider, the project comes from the personal collection of Jobs’ stepbrother, John Chovanec. It had remained at the Jobs family home in Los Altos before eventually becoming part of Chovanec’s collection. That provenance adds another layer of significance for collectors. The object is not simply an old electronics project associated with a famous person; it is a physical artefact from Jobs’ childhood that survived for more than half a century. Its survival also provides a rare look at Jobs before Apple existed. Much of the memorabilia associated with him comes from his professional career, particularly Apple’s early years. This project instead captures a much earlier stage of his life, when his interest in electronics was still developing.Bidding has pushed the project into five figures of interestThe science project is being sold as part of RR Auction’s “Steve Jobs & the Computer Revolution: The Apple 50th Anniversary Auction Part Two”. The auction contains more than 200 lots connected to Jobs, Apple and the history of personal computing. By August 19, bidding on the science project had reached $8,475, with the auction scheduled to close on August 20 at 6 p.m. Eastern Time. The auction house expects the project could ultimately sell for more than $20,000. The rising price reflects the unusual combination of technological history, personal provenance and Jobs’ connection to the object. A school science project might normally have little monetary value, but this one has become a piece of the story behind one of the world's most recognisable technology companies.Other Apple memorabilia is also drawing big bidsThe science project is only one part of the auction. Other lots offer collectors objects from different stages of Apple’s development, including vintage computers, components, advertising material and documents connected to Jobs. Among the more valuable items is an Apple-1 computer housed inside a Smith-Corona typewriter case. A Steve Jobs-signed Apple business card is also included, alongside other early Apple material. The auction follows an earlier sale that demonstrated just how much collectors are willing to pay for important pieces of Apple history. In the first part of the anniversary auction, the first cheque issued by Apple sold for $2.4 million, while an Apple-1 prototype board reached $2.75 million. Against those multimillion-dollar sales, Jobs’ eighth-grade project is a much smaller artefact. Yet its appeal comes from something those later objects cannot provide, it shows the future Apple co-founder before Apple existed.A glimpse of the inventor before AppleThe value of Jobs’ science project ultimately goes beyond the electronics mounted on its wooden display. It captures an early moment in the life of someone who would later have an enormous influence on personal technology. The project does not show the finished products, dramatic launches or corporate milestones that later defined Jobs’ career. Instead, it shows a schoolboy investigating how a semiconductor worked and building a practical demonstration around it. That makes the object particularly compelling as Apple reaches its 50th anniversary. The company’s history is usually told through the Apple-1, Macintosh, iPod, iPhone and other landmark products. This small eighth-grade project offers a much earlier chapter, a physical reminder that the story of Jobs’ technological curiosity began long before the Apple logo became globally recognised. What began as an eighth-grade science experiment has now become a rare piece of technology history, with collectors bidding for a glimpse of Steve Jobs before he became Steve Jobs.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: China sentences Evergrande founder Hui Ka Yan to life in prison for financial crimes
articles.summary: China News: China has sentenced Evergrande founder and former chairman Hui Ka Yan to life in prison for financial crimes linked to the property developer's operat.
articles.body: China has sentenced Evergrande founder and former chairman Hui Ka Yan to life in prison for financial crimes linked to the property developer's operations. The Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court also ordered his assets to be confiscated.According to The New York Times, Hui pleaded guilty in April to charges including fundraising fraud, misuse of funds and securities-related offences. The court said Hui and Evergrande committed financial crimes between 2016 and 2021. Evergrande Group and Evergrande Real Estate Group were fined a combined 15.82 billion yuan, about $2.35 billion.Hui founded Evergrande in Guangzhou in 1996 as China's property market expanded. The company became one of China's largest developers and expanded into businesses including football and electric vehicles.Evergrande relied heavily on borrowing to expand its property business. The company accumulated more than $300 billion in liabilities before defaulting in 2021 after struggling to meet its debt obligations.Beijing had introduced measures in 2020 to limit borrowing by property developers. The restrictions reduced access to financing for highly indebted companies such as Evergrande.The company also faced allegations of financial misconduct. Chinese authorities said Evergrande had overstated revenue and committed securities-related violations. Hui was held responsible for the company's operations during the period covered by the case.A Hong Kong court ordered Evergrande into liquidation in January 2024 after the company failed to present a restructuring plan acceptable to creditors.Evergrande's collapse became part of China's wider property-sector crisis. Property had been a major contributor to China's economic growth, while developers were linked to banks, suppliers, local governments and homebuyers.The property downturn has since affected investment, household wealth and economic activity. Evergrande's failure exposed the risks of a property model based on high borrowing and continued growth in housing demand.The Shenzhen court also sentenced 56 other people in the case, including two of Hui's sons. Their prison terms range from 22 months to 18 years.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1936, Beryl Markham took off from England alone hoping to reach New York; 20 hours later ice starved her engine and she crash-landed in Canada after becoming the first woman to fly the Atlantic solo east-to-west
articles.summary: UK News: On the evening of 4 September 1936 a turquoise-and-silver monoplane left an airfield in Oxfordshire and set out for the Atlantic. Darkness lay ahead. .
articles.body: On the evening of 4 September 1936 a turquoise-and-silver monoplane left an airfield in Oxfordshire and set out for the Atlantic. Darkness lay ahead. So did thousands of miles of open water, brutal headwinds and the chance that the aircraft would never return. Beryl Markham, 33, was at the controls alone in the cockpit, trying for a trip no woman had yet achieved. She was going to New York. Her course was westward across an ocean with prevailing winds that made the crossing particularly unforgiving. Markham fought the elements for about 20 hours. Then, off the coast of Canada, ice clogged the airplane's fuel-tank vents, starving the engine, a plane crashed in a peat bog on Cape Breton Island, states Afterburner magazine report. Markham lived, though she was cut across the forehead. She, too, had made history in aviation.Wild raised in KenyaBeryl Markham was born Beryl Clutterbuck in England in 1902, but her landscape was Africa. At four she moved with her father to colonial Kenya, where he set up a horse-racing farm near the Great Rift Valley. Markham was raised far from the conventions of Edwardian England. She learned to navigate the African wilderness, fell in love with horses at an early age, and hunted with local kids. By age 17 she was training thoroughbreds for a living. But eventually horses would have to share her attention with something even more thrilling: flying.Flying in the sky freedomMarkham had learned to fly under British pilot Tom Campbell Black. She eventually became a bush pilot flying over the vast and often unforgiving expanses of East Africa. Practical as well as adventurous was her work. She flew over the bush looking for elephants and other game, spotting animals from the air and relaying their location on to safaris below. Those flights were an unusual schooling for her. The African wilderness taught Markham to operate without roads, landmarks or immediate help. She learned to trust her own judgment, to keep her cool in the air, all by herself. That experience would prove invaluable as she looked out over the Atlantic Ocean.West in to the niteThe east-west crossing of the Atlantic was particularly daunting. Westbound pilots had to fight the prevailing westerlies for most of the way. Markham chose a Percival Vega Gull, which she named The Messenger, and was to fly from England to Floyd Bennett Field in New York. She left on September 4 into the nite and disappeared. She flew for hours over the ocean. The aircraft fought against fatigue, cold and the relentless Atlantic wind as she carried on through darkness and into the next day.They finally made it to the North American coast after about 20 hours. And then the disaster came, where ice had formed around the vents to the aircraft’s fuel tanks, blocking the engine from getting the fuel it needed. The engine started to die. The destination was so close that Markham had no choice but to put the plane down.A cape breton crashThere was a Vega Gull found in a peat bog in Baleine Cove, Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia. The landing was rough but Markham emerged from the wreckage with a cut on her forehead, and alive. Her intended destination was New York, but she had instead landed in Canada. But the last leg was a failure, and that could not wipe out what she had done. Markham was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic from east to west and the first person to fly nonstop from England to North America.The Book Hemingway could not escapeSeveral years later came Markham's greatest literary venture. In 1942 West with the Nite was published, a memoir that blended memories of Africa, horses, aviation and the landscapes that had defined her life. Its prose was strikingly elegant, vivid, controlled, and atmospheric. But the book attracted little commercial attention at first. It soon went out of print and for decades Markham's literary achievement was forgotten. And then, in 1982, the book found an unlikely champion. A California restaurateur looking through a collection of Ernest Hemingway’s letters found a passage where the famous novelist praised Markham’s writing. Intrigued, he tracked down a copy of West With The Nite and was eager for it to be republished and the gamble paid off. The book was reprinted and became a bestseller and Markham was awarded the recognition she had not received in the decades after her historic flight.An above the record lifeMuch of her life still took up with horses, and she remained in Kenya. She trained racehorses well into her 80s and stayed connected to the world she had known since childhood. But by the time West with the Nite was rediscovered, Markham was an old woman living in reduced circumstances near the Nairobi racetrack. The royalties from the book’s renewed success gave her financial security at last and allowed her to enjoy her final years in comfort. She died in 1986 in Nairobi.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
