articles.title: India, Japan deepen defence ties with maritime security pact; China challenge looms over Indo-Pacific
articles.summary: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh and his Japanese counterpart Shinjirō Koizumi held a bilateral dialogue in New Delhi.
articles.body: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh and his Japanese counterpart Shinjirō Koizumi held a bilateral dialogue in New Delhi. Koizumi is on his maiden visit to India and the visit is seen as an expansion of the 'Special Strategic and Global Partnership' between the two countries, which is gaining importance in light of an assertive China across the Indo-Pacific region. The special strategic partnership, which was formalised in 2014 has continuously been strengthened by the leadership of the two countries, with PM Modi visiting Japan eight times. The strategic relationship has been anchored by shared democratic values and a common vision for a free and open Indo‑Pacific. During the meeting the defence minister of both the nations signed a Memorandum of Arrangement (MoA) on maritime security cooperation. This agreement provides a framework for strengthening cooperation between the naval forces of the two countries information sharing in the realm of maritime domain awareness and Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR).Defence cooperation between New Delhi and Tokyo has accelerated in recent years. A series of agreements since 2014 have institutionalised exchanges, ranging from the Memorandum of Defence Cooperation to the Reciprocal Provision of Supplies and Services pact signed in 2020. This framework has been operationalised during naval wargames such as MILAN and JAIMEX. These exercises have enabled seamless logistics during visit of ships and aircraft alike. The co‑development of Japan's UNICORN integrated communications antenna system for the Indian Navy, a deal that was formalised in 2024, represents the first joint equipment project between the two countries.The current visit has seen the defence ministers of both nations reaffirm their commitment to maritime security cooperation, mine countermeasures and joint shipbuilding. Japan’s technological expertise and India’s production capabilities are being aligned under the “Make in India” framework, with discussions on reciprocal ship repair facilities progressing. The two sides welcomed the expansion of bilateral exercises, including Dharma Guardian and JAIMEX, and looked ahead to Veer Guardian 26, which will see Japanese fighter aircraft participate in India for the first time. Both ministers also emphasised the importance of deepening defence R&D cooperation between Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and Japan’s Acquisition Technology and Logistics Agency (ATLA), and confirmed plans to convene a Defence Industry Forum.The two countries have also decided to accelerate discussions towards convening the Fourth Japan-India foreign and defence ministerial (2+2) meeting that is scheduled to be held in Tokyo later this year. Besides this, Singh and Koizumi are working to further promote cooperation through the Indo-Pacific Logistics Network (IPLN). This initiative supports partner countries during natural disasters by facilitating the transportation of personnel and supplies for humaitarian assistance and disaster relief operations.Beyond defence, the visit reaffirmed the salience of economic security as a foundational pillar of the partnership. The synergy between Japan’s Free and Open Indo‑Pacific vision and India’s Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions (MAHASAGAR) initiative provides strategic impetus to cooperation. Both sides are committed to elevating economic security ties, recognising that prosperity and security are intertwined.The Japanese Defence Minister’s presence in India is thus more than ceremonial. It reflects a partnership that has evolved from cultural affinity into strategic convergence. The two nations have an enduring and rich cultural history, with links dating back to 752 AD, when Bodhisena, an Indian monk, consecrated the Great Buddha at Nara’s Todaiji Temple. In modern times, figures such as Swami Vivekananda, Rabindranath Tagore, Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose and Rash Behari Bose deepened the bonds of friendship. The Japan‑India Association, founded in 1903, is Japan’s oldest international friendship body. From Bodhisena’s consecration at Nara to joint naval drills in the Indian Ocean, the arc of India‑Japan relations is long, resilient and central pillar to keeping the Indo-Pacific open for all.

articles.title: Harvard to pay $53 million after human remains donated to its medical school were stolen and sold on the black market
articles.summary: Harvard University has agreed to pay $53 million to settle civil lawsuits brought by families whose relatives donated their bodies to Harvard Medical
articles.body: Harvard University has agreed to pay $53 million to settle civil lawsuits brought by families whose relatives donated their bodies to Harvard Medical School for research and education, after parts of those donated remains were stolen and sold in a nationwide black-market scheme. The scandal centred on Cedric Lodge, a former manager of Harvard Medical School's morgue, who prosecutors said stole organs, skin, brains and dissected heads from donated cadavers. Lodge transported some of the remains to his home in New Hampshire and sold them to buyers in other states, with some later resold for profit. He pleaded guilty to trafficking stolen human remains and was sentenced to eight years in prison in December 2025. His wife, Denise Lodge, was also sentenced to prison for her role in the scheme.How the Harvard human remains scandal unfoldedLodge had access to cadavers donated through Harvard's Anatomical Gift Program, which provides bodies for medical education and research. Prosecutors said he exploited that access by removing parts of bodies without the knowledge or consent of the university, donors or their families. The conduct covered by his guilty plea occurred from 2018 through at least March 2020. Investigators said the stolen remains included organs, brains, skin, hands, faces and dissected heads. Some were taken from the Boston morgue and moved to Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania. Federal prosecutors said Lodge took some of the remains to his home in Goffstown, New Hampshire, where he and Denise Lodge arranged sales to buyers in other states. The transactions formed part of a wider network rather than an isolated series of sales. Some purchasers subsequently resold what they had obtained, allowing the remains to circulate between different people for profit.Lodge pleaded guilty in May 2025 to interstate transportation of stolen human remains. A federal judge sentenced him to 96 months in prison in December 2025. Denise Lodge received a sentence of 12 months and one day. Other people connected to the investigation have also pleaded guilty or been convicted, with prosecutors pursuing cases involving both the Harvard remains and remains taken from other institutions.Families sued HarvardThe federal investigation became public in 2023, prompting affected families to take legal action against Harvard. Their lawsuits alleged that the university had failed to properly safeguard donated remains and asserted claims including negligence, breach of fiduciary duty and emotional distress. The families argued that their relatives had made anatomical donations for medical purposes and had never consented to their remains being commercially traded.The university's agreement is intended to resolve the civil lawsuits without prolonged litigation. It is separate from Lodge's criminal prosecution, and Harvard has not admitted liability as part of the settlement. The agreement provides a mechanism for compensation while also requiring the university to take several additional steps concerning its anatomical donation programme.Who is covered by the settlementThe settlement uses an eligibility period that extends beyond the specific period covered by Lodge's guilty plea. It applies to eligible donors whose remains passed through Harvard's Anatomical Gift Program between January 1, 2018, and March 31, 2023. Qualifying relatives will be able to seek compensation according to the terms of the agreement, although payments remain subject to the settlement process and final court approval.Harvard promises changes and a scholarshipHarvard Medical School has agreed to communicate directly with claimant families through a live webinar and acknowledge that Lodge's conduct was "morally reprehensible" and inconsistent with the university's standards. The school will also provide information about changes made to its Anatomical Gift Program. In addition, Harvard plans to establish an annual financial-aid scholarship for medical students from the 2027-28 academic year in recognition of anatomical donors.The case involving Lodge was one part of a broader federal investigation into the trafficking of human remains. Prosecutors charged several other people who were accused of buying, selling or transporting remains. Some cases involved material taken from Harvard, while others concerned remains stolen from different facilities. The investigation exposed a network in which remains could be moved across state lines and resold between participants.The case has drawn widespread attentionThe scandal is particularly disturbing because anatomical donation relies on the confidence of donors and their families. People who make such donations expect their bodies to be treated respectfully and used for legitimate medical or scientific purposes. The alleged commercial trafficking therefore represented a serious violation of the trust placed in the institution responsible for handling those remains.The settlement has not yet reached its final stage. A court hearing on final approval is scheduled for December 9, 2026. If approved, the agreement will resolve the civil claims covered by its terms. The criminal sentences imposed on Lodge and other defendants remain separate from the settlement, while Harvard has said that addressing the consequences of the scandal and rebuilding trust with affected families will continue.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1624, a family bought an English estate that still contains ancient oak trees from a royal hunting forest; 402 years later some are still standing
articles.summary: In 1624, London lawyer William Anson bought a moated medieval manor at Shugborough in Staffordshire from Thomas Whitby for around £1,000, beginning a
articles.body: In 1624, London lawyer William Anson bought a moated medieval manor at Shugborough in Staffordshire from Thomas Whitby for around £1,000, beginning a family connection with the estate that would last for roughly three centuries. The property had previously belonged to the Bishops of Lichfield before passing through several owners following the Dissolution of the Monasteries, while the surrounding landscape formed part of Cannock Chase, a former royal hunting forest governed by centuries of forest laws. Anson's descendants would eventually transform the modest manor into the grand Shugborough estate visitors know today, but some of the landscape's most remarkable survivors are considerably older than the family itself. Veteran oak trees across Cannock Chase have been recorded at more than 400 years old, meaning some were already growing when Anson purchased Shugborough in 1624. More than four centuries later, these ancient trees remain living reminders of a landscape that has outlasted generations of owners and changing ideas of land use. These remarkable oaks stand as living witnesses to centuries of English history, connecting the medieval past with present conservation efforts to preserve them.How William Anson's 1624 purchase shaped Shugborough for three centuriesAccording to the National Trust's official history of Shugborough Estate, the property had a complicated history before William Anson acquired it in 1624. The original manor associated with the Bishops of Lichfield passed through several owners following the Dissolution of the Monasteries before eventually coming into the hands of Thomas Whitby, who sold it to Anson. A later generation of the Anson family replaced the earlier manor house with a brick residence that formed the basis of Shugborough Hall, which developed over the following centuries. The estate underwent an even greater transformation in the 18th century under Thomas and George Anson. George's successful naval career, including his circumnavigation of the globe and the capture of a Spanish treasure galleon, brought wealth that helped finance Thomas's ambitious expansion of the house, gardens and wider landscape.Why Cannock Chase still has oak trees older than the Anson family's Shugborough connectionThe age of some of the area's veteran oaks provides a striking contrast with the 402-year history of the Anson family's ownership. Cannock Chase had already been protected as a royal hunting forest for centuries before William Anson purchased Shugborough, with forest laws restricting how the land and its resources could be used. Today, some veteran oak trees on Cannock Chase are estimated to be more than 400 years old, placing their earliest growth around or before the period when Anson acquired the estate. Their importance is not simply historical. Ancient and veteran trees provide habitats that younger trees cannot easily replicate, particularly where trunks contain cavities, hollow sections, dead wood and decaying branches. These features can support fungi, lichens, insects and other organisms that depend on old trees and the gradual process of decay. As a result, allowing veteran trees to survive through their later stages of life can be just as important for biodiversity as planting new trees.How Shugborough's ancient trees are being protected for the futureShugborough eventually passed into National Trust care after the death of the 4th Earl of Lichfield in 1960, when the estate was transferred to the Trust in lieu of death duties. Management of the estate later returned fully to the National Trust in 2016 after decades under lease to Staffordshire County Council. Today, conservation work extends beyond protecting the historic buildings and formal landscape. The National Trust has worked with organisations including the Woodland Trust and the Cannock Chase National Landscape partnership to train volunteers to identify and record veteran trees as part of the Ancient Tree Inventory. The wider conservation effort also includes restoring wood pasture, helping create the open conditions young oaks need to develop into mature trees rather than allowing them to become crowded out by surrounding vegetation. That work is aimed at ensuring that Shugborough's tree legacy does not end with the current generation of ancient oaks. Some of the trees standing today may have witnessed the arrival of the Anson family itself; the goal now is to give future trees the chance to remain part of the landscape for centuries more.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: A Belgian car salesman has gone from ordinary life to royal status after Prince Laurent formally recognised him as his son, bringing a long-hidden paternity story into the Belgian royal family.Clément Vandenkerckhove, 26, is the son of Prince Laurent and Belgian singer Wendy Van Wanten. The relationship between Laurent and Van Wanten took place before the prince married Princess Claire in 2003.Vandenkerckhove was quietly brought into Laurent’s family at a town hall ceremony six months ago, although details of his new status have only now emerged.Vandenkerckhove had known for years that Laurent was his biological father. His mother revealed the identity to him when he was 16, and four years later he contacted the prince himself.The pair eventually underwent a DNA test together, which showed a 99.5% match, according to Vandenkerckhove’s account in a Flemish TV documentary.Although the recognition makes him a prince, Vandenkerckhove will not enter the Belgian line of succession, unlike Laurent’s other children, Princess Louise, Prince Aymeric and Prince Nicolas.He will also not undertake official royal duties or receive a royal allowance.He has said he is unsure whether he will adopt the royal family name, Saxe-Coburg, saying he remains proud of his mother’s surname, Vandenkerckhove.The story mirrors that of Laurent’s father, former King Albert II, who was forced to undergo a DNA test after a lengthy paternity dispute.Albert eventually acknowledged artist Delphine Boël as his daughter in 2020, after years of legal battles. She subsequently received the title of princess and adopted the name Delphine de Saxe-Coburg.Belgian law limits public royal allowances to only a handful of members of the royal family, including King Philippe, former King Albert II, Prince Laurent and Princess Astrid.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US debt crosses $40 trillion but everyone still trusts Uncle Sam. But for how long?
articles.summary: US News: TOI correspondent from Washington: The United States’ national debt crossed $40 trillion on Tuesday, a number so large that even breaking it up with c.
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: The United States’ national debt crossed $40 trillion on Tuesday, a number so large that even breaking it up with commas can scarcely make it comprehensible. As in a 4 followed by 13 zeroes: $40,000,000,000,000!Number-crunching economists reached for various metrics to convey the scale of the crisis. The US economy produces roughly $33 trillion worth of goods and services a year. So the debt is now bigger than the entire annual economic output (GDP) of the country. Per American, that works out to roughly $118,000; for a family of four, about $472,000. Divvying it another way, the US is adding debt at a rate of roughly $90,000 every second.To put that in perspective for readers in India, the $40 trillion debt America has racked up is roughly 10 times the size of India’s entire annual economy. In other words — although debt versus GDP is not an apples-to-apples comparison — the US owes roughly ten times the value of everything India produces in a year. America’s debt mountain is therefore not merely bigger than India’s economy; it is about ten Indian economies stacked on top of one another.Economists also put the best possible spin by pointing out that the raw number itself is less important than debt relative to the size of the economy and the government’s ability to service it. Just the US debt held by its public is roughly equal to annual GDP, and the Congressional Budget Office says that, under current law, the ratio could rise to 120% of GDP by 2036 and 175% by 2056.So how did the world’s richest country get here? In the simplest terms, Washington has been spending more than it collects in taxes — year after year, administration after administration. Wars, tax cuts, the 2008 financial crisis, Covid stimulus, an ageing population and rising Social Security and Medicare costs have all added to the bill. The pandemic was particularly spectacular: debt exploded as the government tried to prevent an economic catastrophe.But the extraordinary thing is that America has continued borrowing heavily even after the emergencies have passed. Federal budget deficits are still running at levels normally associated with wars or recessions. The awkward question for Washington now is whether the borrowing eventually stops gently — or with a crash.So who is lending America $40 trillion? Surprisingly, America is not mainly borrowing from China. The biggest lenders are actually Americans and American institutions – pension funds, mutual funds, banks, insurance companies, households and investment funds. Foreign governments and investors also buy what is euphemistically called “US Treasury securities”: Japan held about $1.12 trillion in June, Britain about $940 billion, China about $633 billion and India roughly $200 billion.But why lend to a country this deeply in debt? Because US “Treasury securities” remain the world’s favourite financial equivalent of a steel safe with a very large lock. They are highly liquid, easily traded and backed by the world’s largest economy — as well as by Washington’s long-established record of paying its debts. In other words, America has been able to borrow on an extraordinary scale because the world keeps saying: Yes, Uncle Sam, we’ll take your IOU. For now.President Trump has repeatedly promised to reduce the national debt, including by using tariff revenue. But the arithmetic has not exactly been taking orders from the White House. Amid the irresistible American urge to splurge, Trump is proposing a $1.5 trillion military budget, roughly a 50% increase from recent levels and an unprecedented level of Pentagon spending, arguing that a stronger military is essential to national security.So America is essentially trying to lose weight while ordering a second dessert; spending like a drunken sailor on shore leave — and then promising the bartender that tariffs will somehow pay the tab.And debt is not merely about the amount borrowed. It is also about the interest bill. Interest payments are now approaching $1 trillion a year. That means an increasing share of the federal budget is going simply toward servicing yesterday’s borrowing rather than paying for today’s schools, roads, defence, healthcare or anything else Washington wants to spend money on.As the debt grows, investors could eventually demand higher interest rates to keep buying Treasury securities. That would feed through into mortgage rates, business borrowing costs and the government’s own financing costs, potentially slowing investment and economic growth. The US would then face the unpleasant menu economists have been warning about for years: higher taxes, slower spending, cuts to benefits, faster economic growth, inflation — or some combination of all of them.Washington would have to bring spending and revenues into better balance: restrain the growth of entitlement programmes, control discretionary spending, reconsider tax cuts, raise more revenue and — hardest of all — persuade voters that there is no painless option. There is no magic button marked “Pay Off $40 Trillion.”The CBO’s is essentially warning that the longer Washington waits, the more painful the eventual adjustment becomes. That is America’s peculiar fiscal paradox: the world’s richest country can afford an enormous debt — until one day the debt becomes so enormous that it starts deciding what the world’s richest country can afford. Or as one economist might put it, there is no such thing as a free lunch -- just a lunch somebody has put on the national credit card.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1911, Norwegian whalers released 10 reindeer on South Georgia for food and hunting; a century later nearly 7,000 were removed after the herds damaged native vegetation
articles.summary: Rest of World News: When Norwegian whalers brought ten reindeer to the sub-Antarctic island of South Georgia in 1911, the plan was simple: provide a steady supply of fres.
articles.body: When Norwegian whalers brought ten reindeer to the sub-Antarctic island of South Georgia in 1911, the plan was simple: provide a steady supply of fresh meat and give workers a reminder of home. A century later, that small livestock release had become a major environmental problem, forcing authorities to carry out one of the largest invasive species removal projects in the polar region. The Government of South Georgia & the South Sandwich Islands (GSGSSI), with research published through the Environment & Society Portal’s Arcadia series, documented how the lack of natural predators allowed the reindeer population to grow unchecked. Glaciers kept the animals in the island’s most fertile coastal areas, where they steadily damaged vegetation and threatened native wildlife. In a multi-year effort involving indigenous Sami herders and Norwegian marksmen, officials removed nearly 7,000 reindeer from the British Overseas Territory, allowing damaged habitats to begin recovering.A century of uncontained growthThe first herd was released on the Barff Peninsula by whaler Carl Anton Larsen and other whalers. More releases between 1909 and 1925 created herds in two separate parts of the island. While land-based whaling stations were operating, regular hunting helped keep the numbers under control. That changed after the whaling stations closed in the mid-20th century. Herd management stopped, leaving the reindeer without natural predators or regular human control. Their numbers grew quickly, and by the early 2010s, surveys found several thousand animals spread across the island’s snow-free coastal plains. South Georgia’s rugged interior is dominated by glaciers and high mountains, restricting reindeer to narrow, ice-free coastal areas. These coastal habitats also supported some of the island’s richest plant and wildlife communities.Vegetation loss and soil erosionAs the reindeer population increased, the animals consumed much of their available food. GSGSSI records show that heavy grazing damaged important native plants, including tussac grass (Parodiochloa flabellata) and burnet (Acaena magellanica). Tussac grass can grow taller than a person and provides important shelter for wildlife. In areas heavily used by reindeer, however, thick tussac stands were reduced to bare ground as the animals grazed and trampled the vegetation. The loss of plants also caused widespread soil erosion. Rain washed away thin layers of topsoil from exposed slopes, making the fragile landscape even more unstable. The damage also affected native birds. Burrowing seabirds such as white-chinned petrels and blue prions lost important nesting areas when reindeer trampling damaged their underground burrows. Some remaining nest entrances were left exposed to weather and predators. Non-native plants, especially annual meadow-grass (Poa annua), also spread quickly through the disturbed soil, further changing the native ecosystem.The two-stage eradication campaignFaced with continuing habitat damage, GSGSSI began a formal consultation and decided in 2010 to remove all the reindeer. The operation was carried out in two main phases in different parts of the island. The first phase took place in early 2013 in the Busen region. A specialist team included ten indigenous Sami herders, four Norwegian marksmen, scientists, veterinary staff and support crews. In flatter areas, the Sami herders gathered about 1,000 reindeer into temporary corrals, where the animals were humanely slaughtered under veterinary supervision. In nearby rugged areas, Norwegian marksmen shot groups that could not be safely herded. Officials also made sure the meat was not wasted. More than 7,600 kilograms of inspected reindeer meat was recovered during the Busen operation and later sold to restaurants in the Falkland Islands and cruise ships operating in the region. The second phase focused on the Barff Peninsula and Royal Bay in early 2014. Steep cliffs, rough ground and a lack of safe places to operate herding equipment made corralling impractical, so teams used ground shooting instead. Working from temporary camps supported by the fishery patrol vessel Pharos SG, six Norwegian marksmen searched the Peninsula and removed 3,140 reindeer over six weeks. Across both phases, including earlier culls, nearly 7,000 reindeer were removed, bringing a century of introduced reindeer on South Georgia to an end.Ecosystem recovery under wayRemoving the herds opened the way for wider environmental recovery on South Georgia. Soon after the reindeer operation ended, authorities also completed a major project to remove invasive brown rats, helping restore the island’s coastal habitats. Botanical monitoring in former grazing areas has shown native tussac grass and burnet returning to damaged slopes. As plant roots begin holding the soil together again, ground-nesting seabirds have also started returning to restored burrowing areas. According to records from the Government of South Georgia & the South Sandwich Islands, removing the non-native grazers has allowed plant communities damaged by decades of grazing to recover naturally, without the need for continued human intervention, giving South Georgia’s fragile ecosystems a chance to rebuild and thrive once again. articles.title: Major UK hotel chain CEO Joanna Boydell resigns amid security failings, sexual assault cases
articles.summary: UK News: Joanna Boydell resigns as CEO of Travelodge following security failings and sexual assault incidents involving guests. The hotel chain is under scrutiny for its room key policies, with calls for improved safety measures.
articles.body: A major UK hotel chain's chief executive has stepped down amid growing scrutiny over security failures.Travelodge CEO Joanna Boydell resigned on August 17, the company confirmed in a statement on Thursday. She has been replaced on an interim basis by chief financial officer Ray Reidy, while the company searches for a permanent successor.The resignation follows several reported incidents involving guests receiving room keys without proper checks. In one case, a woman staying at a Travelodge in Maidenhead was sexually assaulted in December 2022 after a man falsely told staff he was her partner and obtained a key to her room. Kyran Smith was later jailed for more than seven years for the attack.Another woman staying at a Travelodge hotel in London while trying to escape a domestic abuser was attacked after reception staff gave the man a key. He reportedly told staff that his girlfriend was upstairs having a seizure. Staff did not check with the woman before giving him access.The woman later told the BBC she ran downstairs “shaking, crying and begging for help”, adding: “I thought someone would protect me.”The incidents have prompted an independent review of Travelodge's security arrangements, led by barrister Paul Greaney KC.The chain also faced political pressure. In March, then-prime minister Sir Keir Starmer wrote to Boydell urging her to “seriously engage” with MPs and the government over concerns about guest safety.Travelodge said Boydell's departure would not affect its efforts to improve security.Chair Stephen Shurrock said the announcement “does not change anything about our focus on safety and security”.The company has since introduced tighter rules for room access. It said any additional or replacement key now requires explicit permission from the guest staying in the room.Travelodge has also checked all its UK rooms to ensure they have a secondary deadbolt and is training around 12,000 customer-facing employees across more than 600 hotels on the revised security policy.The company said it had brought in a specialist on violence against women and girls to train senior executives and review its existing procedures.Reidy said: “We remain focused on the safety and well-being of our guests and will continue taking the actions necessary to strengthen the business.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: For generations, Indonesia’s Huaulu community hunted endangered cockatoos for a sacred ritual; now they use naturally shed feathers
articles.summary: Rest of World News: On Indonesia’s Seram Island, the Huaulu Indigenous community has adapted a centuries-old coming-of-age ritual to reduce hunting pressure on the endang.
articles.body: On Indonesia’s Seram Island, the Huaulu Indigenous community has adapted a centuries-old coming-of-age ritual to reduce hunting pressure on the endangered salmon-crested cockatoo. The Cidaku ceremony marks young men’s transition to adulthood and traditionally involved hunting the cockatoo for its distinctive crest feathers, which are worn in a ceremonial headdress called the puheliam. A new study in the Journal of Ethnobiology titled Sacred Rituals and Endangered Birds: A Biocultural Approach to Cockatoo Conservation on Seram Island, Indonesia, documents how the community, working with researchers and conservation authorities, agreed to replace hunted feathers with naturally moulted ones collected from rescue and rehabilitation centres and zoos. The change allows the ceremony to continue while removing the need to kill wild cockatoos for feathers. Researchers say the approach illustrates how conservation can work with Indigenous cultural traditions rather than simply imposing outside restrictions. However, they stress that the arrangement addresses only one source of pressure, while illegal wildlife trafficking and habitat loss remain much larger threats to the species. This innovative collaboration demonstrates how cultural preservation and wildlife conservation can successfully coexist when researchers and Indigenous communities work together toward mutually respectful solutions.Why the Cidaku ceremony traditionally used salmon-crested cockatoo feathersFor generations, young Huaulu men demonstrated their passage into adulthood through the Cidaku ritual, in which salmon-crested cockatoo feathers formed an important part of the ceremonial puheliam headdress. The symbolism is deeply rooted in Huaulu spiritual traditions: the community views the forest as a living realm inhabited by powerful spirits, and hunting is understood as a sacred exchange rather than simply a means of obtaining an animal or its feathers. The cockatoo became one of the ritual’s important animal targets after earlier traditions associated with head-taking were suppressed by colonial authorities and Christian missionaries in the early 20th century. The research describes the subsequent adaptation as part of a much longer history of cultural change, with the ritual retaining its spiritual significance while its specific practices evolved.Why conservation laws created a conflict with the traditionThe salmon-crested cockatoo (Cacatua moluccensis) is endemic to the Maluku Islands and is classified as Endangered on the IUCN Red List. Its populations have declined sharply, with researchers identifying demand from the illegal wildlife trade as the primary driver, alongside habitat loss from logging and agriculture. The species has disappeared from the nearby islands of Haruku, Saparua and Nusa Laut, leaving Seram as its main remaining stronghold. Indonesian law also gives the bird strict national protection, prohibiting its capture, possession or killing, including for ceremonial purposes. That created a difficult conflict for the Huaulu: enforcing wildlife law protected the cockatoo but could also threaten a ritual central to the community’s cultural and spiritual identity. The researchers therefore explored whether the material used in the ceremony could change without removing the ceremony’s deeper meaning.How naturally shed feathers created a compromiseResearchers worked with the Huaulu community in two main periods, from March to November 2019 and again from July 2024 to May 2025 after the COVID-19 pandemic interrupted the project. They interviewed community members, surveyed households and consulted traditional leaders, hunters and conservation authorities. The resulting agreement uses naturally moulted cockatoo feathers obtained through rescue centres, rehabilitation facilities and zoos instead of feathers taken from hunted birds. The study describes this as a form of symbolic substitution: the feathers retain their cultural and ceremonial importance, while the hunt itself is no longer necessary to obtain them. The agreement also revives traditional forest taboos and customary rules against commercial wildlife exploitation. Researchers caution, however, that this solution does not by itself resolve the cockatoo’s wider conservation crisis. Illegal wildlife trafficking and habitat loss remain major threats, meaning long-term protection will require both community-led conservation and broader action against commercial exploitation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: Meliza Campos-Sanchez has suddenly become the focus of widespread attention after disturbing videos allegedly posted to her social media account became part of a police investigation in Miami-Dade. The 26-year-old influencer and realtor, who built an online audience around lifestyle, family and real estate content, was arrested after authorities investigated a kitchen fire and alleged incidents involving her two young daughters. She now faces serious criminal charges.Who is Meliza Campos-Sanchez?Campos-Sanchez is a 26-year-old social media personality and real estate agent who used Instagram to share glimpses of her family life, beauty content, lifestyle posts and work in property sales. Her online presence had attracted tens of thousands of followers, with her children occasionally appearing in her content.That public image changed dramatically after authorities investigated a fire at her Miami-area home on August 16. Campos-Sanchez was arrested the following day and charged with first-degree arson, child abuse and two counts of child neglect, according to reports based on arrest documents.Police say videos posted online became an important part of the investigation. One allegedly showed Campos-Sanchez handling melted candle wax around herself and her two daughters, who are six and three years old. Another allegedly showed her wearing a silver-colored mask, spraying a liquid onto clothing and setting the material on fire inside the kitchen.Investigators reportedly recovered items including a lighter, a silver mask, burned material and a bottle believed to have contained an ignitable liquid. The allegations remain part of an active criminal case, and Campos-Sanchez is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.What happened to Meliza Campos-Sanchez’s children?The case has also brought attention to Campos-Sanchez’s family circumstances. Her husband, Yusniel Cue, reportedly told investigators that the couple had been experiencing marital problems and that he had been staying with his parents for about a week before the incident. He learned about the social media videos after receiving a call from a friend and contacted authorities.According to the arrest affidavit, the couple’s older daughter told investigators that she and her younger sister saw their mother start the fire. She also reportedly described what happened afterward, including the alleged use of melted candle wax on the children.Cue took custody of the girls after authorities arrived. Reports also say he had previously contacted the sheriff’s office because of concerns about the children’s safety and told investigators about an earlier suicide attempt involving his wife.Campos-Sanchez was taken to a hospital for a mental-health evaluation after the incident and was later booked into the Turner Guilford Knight Correctional Institution after being cleared for release. articles.title: IBM CEO Arvind Krishna on his letter that ‘shocked’ business world, sent company's stock over 25 percent down, making it 'worst day' in IBM history
articles.summary: Tech News News: Facing an impending quarterly earnings miss driven by shifting enterprise IT budgets and rising AI distractions, IBM Chairman and CEO Arvind Krishna o.
articles.body: Facing an impending quarterly earnings miss driven by shifting enterprise IT budgets and rising AI distractions, IBM Chairman and CEO Arvind Krishna opted for radical transparency -- a move that triggered a historic stock plunge but is reported to have aligned with his core leadership philosophy. In an interview with CRN, IBM CEO Krishna detailed the high-stakes decision to pre-announce the 115-year-old tech giant's financial shortfall eight days before its scheduled July 22 earnings call. The disclosure sent IBM shares tumbling more than 25%, marking one of the steepest single-day declines in the company's history.IBM's underperformance stemmed from enterprise clients pausing infrastructure projects to front-load spending on data center hardware amid supply constraints and surging costs. Additionally, Krishna noted that customer attention had been diverted by security debates surrounding an AI model released by Anthropic. He reduced IBM's expected full-year revenue growth for the year by more than $600 million, saying that the fall is in part due to some clients pushing out IBM infrastructure projects to pay for the growing cost of supply constrained memory, storage, servers and other data center infrastructure.Rather than holding the bad news for the standard earnings cycle, Krishna fell back on a long-standing operating principle: "If there’s a hard thing to be done, do it earlier rather than later," Krishna told CRN.Why IBM CEO thinks it was important to ‘tell’ beforehandBy clearing the bad news early, Krishna aimed to pivot the official earnings call away from post-mortem explanations and toward strategic fixes. "Time will tell whether that was the right decision. I tend to think it was," Krishna said. "Otherwise, we would have been spending the last week explaining the hesitation as opposed to what we are going to do to go fix it."The decision highlights the pressures facing IBM as it balances heavy investments in generative AI and long-term quantum computing against Wall Street's short-term expectations. When asked by CRN about potential vulnerability to activist investors or board friction following the market reaction, the CEO, who took the helm in April 2020, remained pragmatic about corporate oversight."If you falter, one should always be just prepared is my view," Krishna said, adding that public CEOs must constantly evaluate whether they are delivering sufficient returns. "And activists, at the end, if I look at the good side, are trying to come in to say, 'I need better returns for clients and for investors.' And if that’s the goal, then one should be prepared to deal with them. That is just the nature of today’s world that we live in."Krishna maintained that his primary strategy to protect the company's innovation roadmap remains centered on client satisfaction and workforce investment.IBM CEO Krishna reasoned the Q2 weakness to deal ‘deferral, and not destruction’. He said, “This was deferral and not destruction.” Krishna made the statement while talking to analysts during IBM’s latest quarterly earnings call with analysts. Krishna’s confidence comes in part from the fact that one-third of those largest infrastructure projects requiring a lot of customer CapEx have already closed.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Why the US is deporting migrants to Liberia instead of their home countries
articles.summary: US News: The United States on Thursday carried out its first deportation under an agreement allowing Liberia to accept up to 1,200 people who are not Liberian .
articles.body: The United States on Thursday carried out its first deportation under an agreement allowing Liberia to accept up to 1,200 people who are not Liberian nationals, marking one of the Trump administration’s largest efforts yet to send deportees to countries other than their own.An initial group of 20 deportees arrived at Roberts International Airport outside Monrovia, according to the news agency Associated Press.The deportees will include nationals from Africa as well as North America, South America and the Caribbean, Liberian information minister Jerolinmek Piah said.Liberian justice minister Natu Oswald Tweh has said those arriving could seek asylum in Liberia if they wished.Liberia calls arrangement humanitarianPiah said the people being sent to Liberia were being received as “guests” and that the arrangement was humanitarian. According to the BBC, he said none of the initial deportees were criminals or facing prosecution in either the US or Liberia.The Liberian government has not disclosed the nationalities of the 20 people who arrived Thursday.Piah said Liberia had “not demanded or received any compensation or promise of rewards” in exchange for agreeing to participate in the programme. He added that the US would provide support to manage the programme and strengthen Liberia's migration system, according to the BBC.Liberia's decision is rooted partly in its history, Piah said, pointing to the country's origins as a settlement for formerly enslaved and freed Black people from the US and the Caribbean.The US State Department declined to answer specific questions about the Liberia agreement but said implementing the Trump administration's immigration policies was a “top priority” and reaffirmed its commitment to ending what it called illegal and mass immigration and strengthening US border security.The Department of Homeland Security declined to confirm Thursday's deportations, citing “operational security reasons”, and referred questions to the State Department.US expands third-country deportation programmeThe Liberia arrangement is part of a wider US policy under President Donald Trump of sending some deportees to countries other than their countries of origin.According to the Third Country Deportation Watch, a partnership between Refugees International and Human Rights First that draws on public records requests, news reports and other sources, the Trump administration has reached agreements with at least 35 countries to accept third-country deportees.More than 23,000 people have been deported to 26 countries under such agreements, according to the organisation.The US State Department previously confirmed that Liberia had agreed to accept people who were not from Liberia. However, a six-page agreement reached in September 2025 and published on the department's website does not specify either the number of people to be accepted or their nationalities.Several African countries have also reached similar arrangements with Washington, including Ghana, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Sierra Leone.Abrego Garcia case highlights third-country policyThe Liberia agreement has also drawn attention because of the case of Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national who was mistakenly deported by the Trump administration to a prison in El Salvador.After being blocked from sending him to his native El Salvador, the administration has said it could deport him to a third country, including Liberia.Abrego Garcia has said he would agree to be sent to Costa Rica, which has said it would accept him. The US government has not sent him there, and he is challenging deportation to Liberia in a federal lawsuit in Maryland.The use of third-country deportations has faced criticism from rights groups, which have raised concerns about migrants being sent to countries where they have no previous connection and where their safety or legal status may be uncertain.The Trump administration has defended the arrangements as lawful.The Liberia agreement is expected to run for a year and could ultimately involve up to 1,200 third-country nationals, making it a significant expansion of Washington's efforts to find alternative destinations for people it seeks to deport.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Around 1830, America imported Japanese wisteria for its hanging purple flowers; the vigorous vines can now smother trees and compete with native vegetation
articles.summary: US News: Explore the journey of Japanese wisteria from a beloved ornamental plant to a damaging invasive species in American forests. Understand its environmental impact and management challenges.
articles.body: Around 1830, Japanese wisteria arrived in the United States as an ornamental plant, prized for its long, fragrant clusters of purple flowers. Wisteria floribunda was planted around homes, gardens and porches because of its striking spring display. For generations, it remained a popular garden vine. But some plants escaped cultivation and reached nearby forests, where the same vigorous growth that made wisteria attractive in gardens gave it a very different role. The USDA Forest Service identifies Japanese wisteria as a nonnative invasive vine and places its introduction to the United States around 1830.Once it reaches a forest, Japanese wisteria can weave through shrubs and climb into the canopy. Its woody stems wrap around trunks and branches, while its dense leaves shade plants growing below. Older vines can become heavy enough to weigh down trees, and tight coils around trunks can limit their growth. The Invasive Plant Atlas notes that Japanese wisteria can girdle trees and shrubs and alter forest vegetation by reducing the light available to native plants.How a garden vine reached the woodsMany infestations have developed close to old gardens and homes, where ornamental vines escaped into surrounding woodland. Japanese wisteria can spread through seeds, but stems that touch the ground can also produce roots and new shoots. That allows a single established plant to spread outward and form a larger patch without relying on new seedlings. Once a vine has reached nearby trees, it can use them as support and move quickly into the canopy.That growth can make the plant particularly difficult to remove. Cutting back the visible vines may leave roots and older stems alive, allowing fresh shoots to appear later. Pulling out a large vine can also be difficult when its stems have become tangled through shrubs and tree branches. In established infestations, land managers often have to return repeatedly to control regrowth.Japanese wisteria is not the only Asian wisteria growing in American landscapes. Chinese wisteria, Wisteria sinensis, was introduced even earlier, and both species now grow outside cultivation in parts of the southeastern United States. Because the two species can hybridise, some wild plants may show a mixture of their characteristics, making identification and management more difficult. For forests, the key point is the same: once these vigorous vines escape into natural areas, they can spread far beyond the garden where they were planted.When ornamental flowers signal invasionThe flowers are one of the easiest ways to recognise a wisteria vine, but they do not always identify the species with certainty. Long clusters of purple, pink or white blooms hang from the vine in spring, which is one reason these plants became popular with gardeners. Distinguishing Japanese wisteria from Chinese wisteria or hybrids may require examining additional features, such as the direction in which the vine twines and the structure of its leaves and flower clusters.Dense vine growth can cover branches, block sunlight and make it difficult for native plants beneath the canopy to compete. Young trees may struggle to grow, while mature trees supporting large vines can become weakened or weighed down. The Alabama Cooperative Extension System recommends repeated cutting and other control measures for invasive wisteria, noting that established plants can be persistent once they have spread into wooded areas. Early detection is therefore important. Small plants can often be removed more easily before their stems reach nearby trees and their roots become established. Once a vine has entered the canopy, control becomes more difficult because managers must protect surrounding vegetation while preventing new growth from returning.Nearly two centuries after Japanese wisteria was introduced for its flowers, the plant is now viewed very differently outside cultivated gardens. Its ability to climb, shade and tightly wrap around other vegetation allows it to spread through forests and compete with native plants. What began as an attractive addition to American landscapes became an invasive vine capable of changing the structure of the forests it invades. The flowers may still be beautiful, but in a forest they can signal that the vine has spread beyond the garden and begun overtaking nearby trees.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2014, New York completed the Javits Center’s bird-safe renovation and green roof; bird collisions fell by more than 90%, while 65 species later used the roof
articles.summary: US News: Discover how the Javits Center's innovative renovations with bird-safe glass and a green roof created a safe haven for birds, reducing collisions by over 90% and attracting 65 species to the roof, transforming urban infrastructure into wildlife-friendly spaces.
articles.body: The Jacob K. Javits Convention Center in Manhattan was once one of New York's most dangerous buildings for birds. Its large glass facade reflected the sky and surrounding vegetation, making the building difficult for migrating birds to see as an obstacle. During the centre's major renovation, completed in the early 2010s, thousands of glass panels were replaced with low-reflection, fritted glass that makes the surface more visible to birds. At the same time, the project added a 6.75-acre green roof, creating a stretch of vegetation high above Manhattan. Monitoring by the NYC Bird Alliance, formerly known as NYC Audubon, found that bird-building collisions at the centre fell by more than 90% after the glass was changed. The roof then became a stopover where migrating birds could feed and rest.The two changes solved different problems. The glass was meant to keep birds from hitting the building, while the roof gave them somewhere to use in a city dominated by concrete, roads and tall buildings. The green roof was planted mainly with sedum and other low-growing vegetation, creating habitat unlike the hard surfaces around it. When biologists began monitoring the roof in 2014, they were not simply checking whether birds visited. They were building a long-term record of which species used the new habitat and how use changed over time.How a glass building became safer for birdsBefore the renovation, the Javits Center was a major collision hotspot. Birds moving through Manhattan during migration could see reflections of trees and sky in the facade and fly toward what appeared to be open space. The renovated building used patterned and less reflective glass instead. The Javits Center's sustainability information says more than 6,000 bird-friendly glass panels were installed and that bird collisions fell by more than 90% after the work.The change did not require removing the building's glass facade altogether. Instead, the new panels incorporated a frit pattern that helped make the surface visible to birds. That approach later became an important example in New York's push for bird-friendly building design. The centre became a case study for how a large glass building could remain useful and visually open while reducing a major danger to migrating birds. The green roof added another part to the story. It turned the top of the convention centre into a patchwork of plants where birds could find insects, shelter and rest. As monitoring continued, the list of recorded species grew.How the green roof became a stopover for birdsOver the years, the roof became more than an experiment in urban landscaping. Birds began using it as a stopover habitat during migration, while resident species also appeared. Monitoring included visual surveys, acoustic recordings and camera traps, allowing researchers to track wildlife that might otherwise have gone unnoticed. By February 2023, NYC Bird Alliance had recorded 51 bird species on the Javits Center’s network of green roofs. Its current project information lists a cumulative total of 65 bird species, along with five bat species and representatives of 18 arthropod orders. The organisation’s records also include native bees, butterflies and other insects.What it can do is offer a small patch of habitat where wildlife can find food and shelter while moving through one of the country's most built-up areas. The researchers have also found signs of interactions between species living there. Their monitoring has included bats feeding on moths, while birds use the vegetation and insects around it. The roof has become a small urban food web, not just a decorative garden.The project also showed why bird-safe glass and green roofs are effective together. Preventing collisions reduces the danger created by the building itself, while the roof gives birds a place to land after they have crossed the city. Neither change solves the wider problem of habitat loss or the many hazards birds face during migration, but together they changed what had once been a particularly hostile part of Manhattan.More than a decade after the renovation, the Javits Center offers an example of how an existing city building can be redesigned for wildlife without losing its original purpose. The convention centre still hosts huge events below, while above it, birds and other animals use a rooftop that did not exist as habitat before the renovation. What started as an effort to reduce collisions became something larger: a building that is safer for birds and a rooftop habitat that supports wildlife during migration. The Javits Center shows that bird-friendly design can serve two purposes at once. Visible glass patterns reduce the chance of fatal collisions, while vegetation above the building provides food, shelter and resting space. The roof cannot replace larger natural habitats, but it demonstrates how urban infrastructure can be redesigned to make room for wildlife.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1966, American folk singer Pete Seeger set out to “build a boat to save the Hudson”; his floating classroom has since reached more than 500,000 people
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Pete Seeger’s Clearwater project transformed the Hudson River from a polluted waterway to a model for environmental education, engaging over 500,000 people in the process.
articles.body: In 1966, when American folk singer Pete Seeger looked at the Hudson River, he did not see the majestic waterway celebrated in songs and paintings. He saw a river overwhelmed by sewage, industrial waste and oil pollution. His response was unusual: instead of starting with a campaign, a lawsuit or a political organisation, Seeger proposed building a wooden sailing boat. The idea was to bring people back to the river, let them experience it up close and persuade them that the polluted waterway was worth saving. Three years later, the 106-foot sloop Clearwater entered the Hudson.According to the Hudson River Maritime Museum, Pete Seeger's interest in the traditional Hudson River sloops grew after his friend Vic Schwarz lent him a copy of Sloops of the Hudson, a 1908 book by William Verplanck and Moses Collyer. By then, no Hudson River sloop remained afloat, with steamships and railroads having displaced the sailing vessels that once carried cargo along the river. Seeger and Schwarz began discussing the idea of building a replica, hoping that bringing one of the historic vessels back to the Hudson could help reconnect people with the river.From folk concerts to a floating classroomThe approach became particularly important because the Hudson's problems were not confined to one source. According to a study published in Soil and Water Conservation, sewage, heavy metals, industrial chemicals and other pollutants had severely damaged the river by the 1960s, helping create a growing public demand for government action. The Clearwater gave people a direct way to experience that environmental crisis. Students and adults could sail the river, examine organisms collected from the water and learn how tides, currents and pollution affected the estuary. Instead of separating environmental education from the landscape being studied, the organisation put the classroom directly on the river.That idea gradually expanded into a wider programme of environmental education. The sloop became a sailing classroom for schoolchildren, a venue for public events and a platform for campaigners. The organisation also used music to bring environmental issues to audiences that might never have attended a conventional conservation meeting.When the boat sailed into politicsThe Clearwater soon moved beyond education. In 1970, Seeger and the crew sailed the newly launched vessel from New York to Washington, DC, carrying a petition and a message about polluted American waterways. During the trip, Seeger and other performers used music and visual presentations to contrast the Hudson’s earlier condition with the polluted river they had come to know. The voyage came at a time when concern over water pollution was becoming increasingly visible in American public life. Environmental groups, local campaigns and federal policymakers were all pushing for stronger action, creating a wider political backdrop for the Clearwater’s journey. The boat became one of many voices drawing attention to the condition of the Hudson and other waterways, helping turn pollution from a local concern into a subject of broader public debate.Historical analysis in Environmental History has described the Hudson as a major arena of modern American environmental activism, where local citizens, politicians and environmental organisations challenged pollution and industrial development. In 1972, Congress passed the Federal Water Pollution Control Amendments, widely known as the Clean Water Act. The law established a national framework for controlling pollution discharged into US waters and marked a major shift towards federal involvement in water protection.The river also began to improve as pollution controls and better sewage treatment reduced many of the discharges that had damaged the Hudson for decades. The change was gradual rather than immediate, and persistent contaminants such as PCBs remained a serious problem. But the river was no longer treated simply as a dumping ground, and efforts to control pollution began to produce measurable improvements in its condition.A boat that outlived its original missionThe most enduring part of Seeger's idea was to make the river itself the centre of environmental education. Since its launch, the Clearwater has carried students, educators and members of the public along the Hudson, turning the river into a classroom as well as a subject of conservation. The vessel was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2004 for its role in the American environmental movement. Its significance lies partly in the unusual combination of history, music, education and activism that shaped the project from the beginning. Seeger's original idea was simple: bring people to the water and give them a reason to care about it.In 1966, Seeger imagined a boat that could help save the Hudson. By 1969, that boat was sailing. More than 50 years later, it is still carrying people onto the river, turning lessons about pollution, ecology and stewardship into something passengers can see, touch and experience for themselves.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Hawaii fenced the summit of Haleakalā against goats and pigs; native plants recovered inside while grazing continued outside
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Haleakalā National Park's innovative fencing efforts have rejuvenated native plant life by excluding invasive species like goats and pigs, showcasing a sustainable conservation success in Hawaii.
articles.body: Picture two patches of the same volcanic landscape, separated by little more than a line of wire fencing. On one side, grazing animals can strip vegetation and disturb the ground. On the other, native plants have a chance to grow without being repeatedly eaten. At the summit of Haleakalā on Maui, that contrast became one of the clearest examples of how simply keeping invasive mammals out can help protect an ecosystem that evolved without them.Haleakalā National Park explains that many of Hawaii's native plants evolved in isolation for millions of years without large grazing mammals. As a result, they often lack the physical or chemical defences that plants elsewhere developed against herbivores. Introduced animals such as feral goats and pigs therefore created a pressure that many native species were never adapted to withstand.The problem was particularly serious in Haleakalā's high-elevation habitats, where rare plants are found nowhere else. Goats browse vegetation and can trample plants, while pigs disturb the soil as they root for food. Keeping these animals away from sensitive areas became an important part of protecting the mountain's native vegetation.How the fence changed the landscapeThe fencing around Haleakalā's summit was not a quick fix. It was part of a long-running conservation effort that developed over decades, with major fencing and animal-removal work taking place during the late 20th century. The basic idea was straightforward: create a physical boundary around sensitive areas, remove feral goats and pigs from within it, and prevent new animals from moving back in.That distinction matters because the fence itself is a legacy of earlier conservation work, rather than something the park is simply putting up today. Maintaining protected areas and controlling animals that breach those boundaries remain part of the wider management challenge, but the major summit fencing effort dates back decades.The ecological logic behind the approach is easier to understand when the two sides of a fence can be compared directly. Where grazing is excluded, plants that would otherwise be repeatedly browsed have a better opportunity to establish and reproduce. Outside protected areas, introduced herbivores can continue to alter vegetation and disturb the ground.The Haleakalā example also sits within a much larger conservation effort across Hawaii. Steven C. Hess's 2016 review in Mammal Study describes invasive mammals as a major driver of ecological change across the Hawaiian Islands, through herbivory, predation and other pressures. The review documents extensive efforts to remove feral goats and pigs from Hawaiian landscapes, alongside efforts to control rats, cats, mongooses and other introduced mammals in places where they threaten native wildlife.Those projects have taken many forms, depending on the species and landscape. Fences have been designed to prevent mammals from entering protected areas, while trapping, hunting and other removal methods have been used to reduce populations already inside. The scale varies from relatively small protected sites to large areas of native habitat.What Haleakalā's fence can teach us?Haleakalā's story is ultimately less about a piece of wire than about removing a pressure that native species never evolved to handle. The mountain's plants developed in an ecosystem largely free of mammalian grazers. Once goats and pigs arrived, they changed that ecological equation.Protecting native habitat therefore requires more than planting rare species or waiting for damaged vegetation to recover. It can also mean stopping the animals that continue to eat, trample or disturb the plants in the first place. Fencing provides one way to create that protection across large and difficult landscapes.The same principle has been used elsewhere in Hawaii, although the species and circumstances differ from those at Haleakalā. Conservation projects on other islands have used predator-proof fencing and intensive animal control to protect seabirds, native forest birds and other vulnerable species. These examples should not be confused with the Haleakalā summit project, but they show how exclusion has become a recurring tool in Hawaiian conservation.For visitors, the lesson is also practical. Haleakalā National Park asks people to help prevent the spread of invasive plants and diseases by staying on designated trails and cleaning boots and equipment before and after visiting sensitive areas. Small actions matter because an isolated island ecosystem can be particularly vulnerable to organisms introduced from elsewhere.The recovery story at Haleakalā is therefore not that a fence magically restored the mountain. It is that removing an ongoing source of pressure gave native vegetation a better chance to survive. Decades after the major summit fencing work began, the protected landscape offers a visible reminder of what can happen when invasive grazing is kept out, and native species are given room to recover.On a mountain where many plants evolved without large grazing mammals, the boundary matters. Inside it, native vegetation has a chance to persist. Outside it, introduced herbivores can continue to shape the landscape. The difference shows why, in some ecosystems, conservation begins with something remarkably simple: deciding what needs to stay out.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1962, five pet mute swans escaped in Maryland; within four decades their descendants neared 4,000 and were eating 10.5 million pounds of Chesapeake Bay grasses a year
articles.summary: US News: In 1962, five mute swans escaped from an estate in Talbot County, Maryland. More than four decades later, their descendants had grown to nearly 4,000 .
articles.body: In 1962, five mute swans escaped from an estate in Talbot County, Maryland. More than four decades later, their descendants had grown to nearly 4,000 in the Chesapeake Bay region. As their numbers rose across the Chesapeake Bay region, so did concerns about how much underwater vegetation they were consuming and how they were affecting native birds.The Maryland Invasive Species Council said in 2005 that the population had more than doubled nine times in 40 years and was approaching another doubling. The US Geological Survey, in a 2002 publication, put the Chesapeake Bay population at about 4,500.Mute swans are native to Europe and Asia and are considered an invasive species in the Chesapeake Bay. They are large white waterfowl, with adults growing up to five feet long, having a wingspan of seven to eight feet and weighing as much as 25 pounds.These swans feed heavily on submerged aquatic vegetation, also known as SAV, which includes underwater grasses such as eelgrass and widgeon grass. The Maryland Invasive Species Council estimated that the region's mute swans were eating about 10.5 million pounds of aquatic grasses every year.A fast-growing populationThe five swans that escaped in 1962 became the starting point of a population that grew rapidly in the Chesapeake Bay region. By the late 1990s, the population had increased sharply. A USGS report said the number had risen by 1,200% between 1986 and 1999.The report also noted that the Chesapeake Bay population represented about 30% of the total Atlantic Flyway mute swan population at the time. Unlike tundra swans, which visit the Chesapeake Bay during winter, mute swans remain in the region throughout the year.That means the birds continue feeding on the Bay's aquatic vegetation during spring and summer. Native waterfowl also eat these grasses, but they are only present in the region for part of the year.The Maryland Invasive Species Council said mute swans could also interfere with efforts to restore aquatic grass beds. The birds can consume new plants that are important for the recovery of these underwater habitats. According to the council, they could wipe out a restoration planting in only a few days.Why underwater grasses matterAquatic grasses are an important part of the Chesapeake Bay ecosystem. The Maryland Invasive Species Council described them as the base of many food chains in the Chesapeake estuary. A range of plants and animals depend on these grasses, including species that are important to commercial activities.Mute swans feed by putting their heads and long necks underwater. They can pull out whole plants, including their roots and rhizomes. The Chesapeake Bay Program says adult mute swans eat more than eight pounds of underwater grasses each day.Their diet includes eelgrass and widgeon grass. The USGS report found that widgeon grass made up 56% of the food found in the birds' gullets, while eelgrass accounted for 43%. Other submerged aquatic vegetation and invertebrates made up a much smaller share.The birds also change their diet at different times of the year. During winter, they can eat wheat and other grains from farm fields. But underwater grasses remain an important food source, particularly during spring and summer.Pressure on native birdsMute swans are known for aggressive behaviour, and the Maryland Invasive Species Council said this had led to native birds being displaced from nesting and feeding areas.The USGS also reported that populations of black skimmers and least terns nesting on beaches and oyster shell bars had been eliminated by molting mute swans.Mute swans can also be highly territorial. The Chesapeake Bay Program says a male becomes particularly protective while the female is incubating eggs and when the cygnets are young. It may hiss at and chase away people and other birds that come too close.Difficult management The rapid growth of the population led Maryland resource managers to consider ways to control mute swan numbers. The issue became controversial, with animal rights groups opposing control measures.The Maryland Invasive Species Council said animal rights groups had argued that state and federal wildlife agencies were using mute swans as a scapegoat for wider environmental problems.The USGS reported that proposed control measures included addling eggs, which prevents eggs from hatching, as well as killing adult swans. The issue also became contentious among some residents of the Chesapeake Bay area.Legal challenges also affected efforts to control the birds. However, by 2005, new legislation passed by Congress had made clear that the invasive species had no federal protection, according to the council. However, animal rights activists said they planned to continue their court challenges.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: UAE is turning desert sand into eco-friendly bricks, and the method cuts  cement needed for construction to nearly half
articles.summary: Middle East News: Dubai is surrounded by dunes and for a country that has ample desert sand, one would think they would utilise it as a resource. However, the sand unde.
articles.body: Dubai is surrounded by dunes and for a country that has ample desert sand, one would think they would utilise it as a resource. However, the sand underfoot has long been a poor fit for ordinary concrete. Wind makes desert grains unusually fine, smooth, and rounded, so they do not interlock as easily as the rougher aggregate commonly drawn from rivers. But research from the University of Sharjah transforms desert sand into eco-friendly bricks, according to a report by EurekAlert! The November 2025 research was published in the Journal of Materials in Civil Engineering and released in February 2026 by the university.An abundant materialIn the study, researchers including Dr Mohamad Arab and Professor Maher Omar combined desert sand collected in the Sharjah region with alkali-activated binders. This technology uses alkaline solutions to trigger chemical reactions capable of forming rigid structures, similar to a resistant mineral matrix.The formulation also incorporates industrial by-products, such as blast furnace slag and industrial ashes. The use of slag and industrial ashes expands the environmental interest of the research. These by-products, when reused in construction materials, can reduce waste and decrease the pressure for conventional raw materials. Instead of relying solely on Portland cement, the proposal makes advantage of materials that can gain new value within the construction industry, reducing the need for inputs with a higher environmental impact.One of the central points of the research is that the bricks were cured at room temperature. This means that the tested process does not require thermal curing or an oven, a step that could increase energy consumption and raise manufacturing costs.Resistance to sulfatesThe bricks underwent durability tests, including water absorption, wetting and drying cycles, efflorescence and sulfate exposure. According to the researchers, the performance met the ASTM standards cited in the study, used as an international reference for material quality and safety. “We also evaluated performance under aggressive chemical exposure and found that the alkali-activated desert sand bricks retained their integrity and, in key cases, outperformed cement-based bricks under sulfate attack. This matters in coastal and marine environments where sulfate-rich soils and groundwater can accelerate deterioration,” said Maher Omar, Professor of Civil Engineering at the University of Sharjah.Sulfate resistance is important because this type of chemical attack can damage construction materials in coastal and marine areas, or with soils and groundwater rich in this compound. In the reported tests, the desert sand bricks maintained integrity and, in some cases, outperformed cement-based bricks.Another point observed by the researchers was the lower water absorption. This indicator is relevant because excessive water ingress can compromise the durability of masonry materials over time, especially in aggressive environments. According to the team, the eco-friendly bricks demonstrated superior mechanical performance to conventional cement-based bricks in some of the tests. This result reinforces the hypothesis that desert sand can cease to be seen only as a problematic material and become part of more resistant technical solutions.Portland cement has high emissionsPortland cement remains one of the most used materials in the world because it combines strength, durability, and wide availability. The problem is that its production has a high climate impact. According to the University of Sharjah’s statement, it is associated with up to 10% of global carbon dioxide emissions. The authors note that construction is “a major contributor to worldwide carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions and climate change,” consuming approximately 40% of global energy.The research does not claim that the new brick will replace cement in all constructions. What the study indicates is an alternative route to reduce dependence on Portland cement in masonry units, especially in places where desert sand is abundant and reusable industrial materials are available.Industrial production a pipe dreamDespite the promising results, the technology is still in an experimental stage. The study shows feasibility in the laboratory, but real adoption depends on tests in larger units, pilot production, quality standardisation, and cost analysis. The researchers also plan to better quantify the environmental benefits and assess the manufacturing logistics. Industrial production will be the decisive test to know if the desert sand brick can compete with alternatives already established in the construction market.“The broader strategic goal is clear: developing building materials that are locally sourced, resilient in harsh environments, and aligned with sustainability objectives, without compromising performance,” said Omar. “We will also quantify the environmental benefits more clearly so we can identify the most practical and scalable pathway for industry adoption,” Prof. Omar maintained.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
